chemistrykit.AdsorptionIsotherm: BETIsotherm generalizes Langmuir to multilayer adsorption. As the saturation vapor pressure P_0 \to \infty at fixed K=C/P_0, multilayer condensation is suppressed and BET reduces exactly to the Langmuir isotherm -- a reduction verified here numerically, not just asserted.

Balandin's multiplet theory (1929) predicted that when catalytic activity is plotted against binding strength across a series of catalysts, it rises, peaks and falls again, tracing a "volcano". Bligaard, Norskov and coworkers (2004) later derived that shape from the Bronsted-Evans-Polanyi relation. This example reproduces the volcano with the standard textbook toy model (Chorkendorff & Niemantsverdriet, Concepts of Modern Catalysis and Kinetics, 2nd ed., Wiley-VCH, 2007, Ch. 8). The rate needs an occupied site to hold the intermediate and an empty site for the next step, so rate \propto\theta(1-\theta), with \theta the Langmuir coverage (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.langmuir.langmuir_coverage). The adsorption constant K stands in for binding strength. A hypothetical series of catalysts sits on the two legs of the volcano, and its summit is exactly Langmuir's half-saturation point K = 1/P. This is not a literal reproduction of Balandin's multiplet equations.
Balandin's volcano curve: catalytic activity peaks at intermediate binding

Polanyi (1914) described adsorption by the potential A = RT\ln(P_0/P) (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.polanyi_potential) and claimed that the filled pore volume depends on A alone, through one characteristic curve that does not change with temperature. Dubinin and Radushkevich (1947) gave that curve for microporous carbons as W = W_0\exp[-(A/E)^2] (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.dubinin_radushkevich_loading). Below, isotherms measured at three temperatures look different against P/P_0 but fall onto a single curve when replotted against A. A Dubinin-Radushkevich fit then recovers the pore volume W_0 and the characteristic energy E (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.fit_dubinin_radushkevich).
Polanyi's potential theory and the Dubinin-Radushkevich characteristic curve

FreundlichIsotherm models the empirical power law q=K_fP^{1/n}, useful for a heterogeneous surface where Langmuir's single-site-energy assumption breaks down. Unlike Langmuir, it has no saturation limit, so extrapolating it far beyond the fitted pressure range is unphysical. fit_freundlich recovers (Kf, n) via the standard log q vs. log P linearization.

LangmuirIsotherm models monolayer adsorption on a fixed pool of identical surface sites. Its fractional coverage \theta=KP/(1+KP) reaches exactly one-half at the half-saturation pressure P=1/K, and fit_langmuir recovers (K, qmax) from noisy loading-vs-pressure data via the standard 1/q-vs-1/P linearization.

chemistrykit.BornLandeLatticeEnergy: Born and Lande (1918) balanced the Madelung attraction -A/r against a short-range repulsion B/r^n; setting dU/dr=0 at the observed spacing r_0 gives U=-\frac{N_AM|z_+z_-|e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0}(1-\frac{1}{n}), which BornLandeLatticeEnergy evaluates. This example shows the energy curve for NaCl and compares the equation with Born-Haber values for six rock-salt halides.
Born-Lande equation: lattice energies of the alkali halides

Kapustinskii (1956) replaced the structure-specific Madelung constant with a near-universal constant per ion, so KapustinskiiLatticeEnergy needs only the number of ions per formula unit, the charges, and the ionic radii. On rock-salt halides it tracks the structure-based Born-Lande value; it also handles salts of other structures (fluorite CaF2) where no Madelung constant is supplied at all.
Kapustinskii equation: lattice energy without a crystal structure

chemistrykit.Buckingham: The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

chemistrykit.CatalyticRateComparison: In 1823 Doebereiner found that spongy platinum ignites a jet of hydrogen in air at room temperature and comes out of the reaction unchanged; in 1835 Berzelius named the phenomenon catalysis. This example makes both halves of that observation quantitative with illustrative (not measured) parameters for 2H_2 + O_2 \to 2H_2O. Lowering the activation energy on platinum (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.catalysis.compare_catalyzed_rate) turns a reaction that is frozen at room temperature into a fast one, and the turnover_number keeps growing while the amount of platinum stays exactly the same. The catalyst is used again and again, never used up.
Doebereiner's platinum and Berzelius's catalysis: a catalyst that is not consumed

Arrhenius's k = Ae^{-E_a/RT} explains why a catalyst's lower activation energy multiplies the rate by e^{\Delta E_a/RT} (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.catalysis.compare_catalyzed_rate). Ostwald's definition adds the key condition that a catalyst cannot move the equilibrium. It lowers the barrier for the forward and the reverse reaction by the same amount, so both rate constants grow by the same factor and K = k_f/k_r does not change. Below, the reversible reaction A \rightleftharpoons B reaches equilibrium far sooner with the catalyst, and it reaches exactly the same equilibrium.
Arrhenius and Ostwald: a catalyst speeds a reaction but leaves its equilibrium alone

Plotting \ln P against 1/T gives a straight line of slope -\Delta H_{vap}/R; from_two_points recovers \Delta H_{vap} from two measured points, and boiling_point inverts the curve to find the boiling point at altitude.
The Clausius-Clapeyron vapor-pressure curve of water

Gibbs's phase rule, F = C - P + 2 (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.phase_equilibria.gibbs_phase_rule), says how many intensive variables can change while a set of phases coexists. On a one-component phase diagram, single-phase regions are areas (F=2), two-phase boundaries are curves (F=1), and three phases meet only at a point (F=0). The sketch below draws water's diagram around its triple point (vaporization and sublimation curves from the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, melting line from the Clapeyron slope) and labels each feature with its degrees of freedom.

chemistrykit.EigenstateResult: Hund and Mulliken's molecular-orbital theory builds one-electron orbitals spread over the whole molecule as a linear combination of atomic orbitals, \psi_\pm=c_A\chi_A\pm c_B\chi_B. H2PlusVariational does this for H2+ with one Gaussian orbital per proton: diagonalizing the 2x2 problem gives the in-phase bonding orbital (equal coefficients, energy below the isolated-atom level) and the out-of-phase antibonding orbital (opposite coefficients, energy above it). Following both orbital energies from short bond lengths out to separated atoms gives Mulliken's correlation diagram for the simplest molecule.
Hund-Mulliken LCAO molecular orbitals of H2+: bonding and antibonding

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.

chemistrykit.EquationOfState: Clapeyron's 1834 combined gas law unites Boyle's law (PV constant at fixed T), Charles's and Gay-Lussac's law (V \propto T at fixed P), and Avogadro's hypothesis into PV_m = RT. This example draws both classic views with IdealGas: hyperbolic Boyle isotherms, and straight Charles isobars that all extrapolate to zero volume at absolute zero.

Redlich and Kwong divided van der Waals's attraction term by \sqrt{T}. This example draws CO2 P-V isotherms well above and just below the critical temperature from RedlichKwong, with VanDerWaals and IdealGas for comparison. Both real-gas equations are built from CO2's critical temperature and pressure alone via from_critical_constants. Redlich-Kwong's universal critical compressibility factor is 1/3, closer to real gases than van der Waals's 3/8.
Redlich-Kwong isotherms of CO2 against van der Waals and the ideal gas

Peng and Robinson tuned the temperature dependence of their attraction term, \alpha(T), to Pitzer's acentric factor \omega so that the equation reproduces pure-fluid vapor pressures. This example computes the CO2 vapor-pressure curve predicted by PengRobinson (\omega = 0.224) with saturation_pressure, and compares it with van der Waals and Redlich-Kwong built from the same critical constants. Only Peng-Robinson passes through Pitzer's defining point, \log_{10}(P_{sat}/P_c) = -1 - \omega at T/T_c = 0.7.
Peng-Robinson: vapor pressures from the acentric factor

G. N. Lewis replaced pressure by the fugacity f = \phi P so that the ideal-gas form \mu = \mu^\circ + RT\ln(f/P^\circ) stays exact for real fluids. The left panel shows the fugacity coefficient \phi of supercritical CO2 computed by fugacity_coefficient from three equations of state. The right panel shows Lewis's phase-equilibrium criterion: below T_c the liquid and vapor fugacities from fugacity cross exactly at the saturation pressure.
Lewis fugacity: the effective pressure of a real gas

van't Hoff found that a dilute solution's osmotic pressure (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.osmotic_pressure) equals the pressure the solute particles would exert as an ideal gas at the same concentration and temperature. The factor i counts particles per formula unit: 1 for sucrose, about 2 for NaCl. The same factor multiplies the other colligative effects, freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.freezing_point_depression, boiling_point_elevation).
van't Hoff's osmotic pressure law, Pi = iMRT

chemistrykit.EquilibriumComposition: For N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 the reaction quotient Q = x_{NO_2}^2/x_{N_2O_4} (at P = P^\circ), computed by reaction_quotient, rises monotonically with the extent of reaction. The law of mass action says the mixture stops changing where Q reaches the equilibrium constant K. Starting from different mixtures of reactant and product, the equilibrium compositions found by solve_equilibrium_composition all give the same Q = K.
Guldberg and Waage's law of mass action: Q = K at equilibrium

Gibbs showed that at fixed temperature and pressure a system reaches equilibrium at the minimum of its total Gibbs energy G = \sum_i n_i\mu_i. For N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 this example plots G(\xi) from gibbs_energy_of_mixture at several temperatures and marks the composition returned by solve_equilibrium_composition, which sits at each minimum. The slope dG/d\xi = \sum_i\nu_i\mu_i (the reaction Gibbs energy) crosses zero there.
Gibbs's equilibrium criterion: minimum total Gibbs energy

chemistrykit.FirstOrder: van't Hoff (1884) classified reactions by the order n of their rate law -d[A]/dt = k[A]^n. The three textbook cases -- ZeroOrder, FirstOrder, and SecondOrder -- all started from the same initial concentration and with rate constants chosen to give the same half-life, so the different curvature (linear, exponential, hyperbolic) is the only thing distinguishing them. First order is the only one whose half-life doesn't depend on the starting concentration; the plot below marks all three half-lives to make that concrete.

Wilhelmy (1850) followed the acid-catalyzed inversion of cane sugar by polarimetry: the optical rotation \alpha(t) drifts from the dextrorotatory sucrose value towards the (levorotatory) value of the glucose + fructose mixture. Because \alpha is linear in the concentrations, \alpha(t) - \alpha_\infty is proportional to the sucrose still present, and a straight line of \ln[(\alpha - \alpha_\infty)/(\alpha_0 - \alpha_\infty)] against t identifies -d[\text{sugar}]/dt = k[\text{sugar}].

chemistrykit.GaussianPrimitive: S. F. Boys (1950) proposed building molecular wavefunctions from Gaussian functions e^{-\alpha r^2} instead of the physically natural Slater-type e^{-\zeta r}. The payoff is the Gaussian product theorem: the product of two Gaussians on different centres is a single Gaussian on a point between them, so every multi-centre integral reduces to a closed form. This example checks the theorem numerically, checks the closed-form overlap integral (~chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets.overlap_integral) and the Boys function (~chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets.boys_f0) against brute-force quadrature, and shows the price paid: one Gaussian has no cusp at the nucleus, while a contraction of three (STO-3G) comes close to the Slater 1s orbital.
Boys's Gaussian-type orbitals and the Gaussian product theorem

Roothaan and Hall turned the molecular orbital problem into matrix algebra: expand each orbital in a finite, non-orthogonal basis and the variational condition becomes the generalized eigenvalue problem HC=SCE, solved here by solve_secular_equation. For the one-electron H2+ the Fock matrix is just the core Hamiltonian, so the equation is solved exactly once in each basis. The example shows that the overlap matrix S matters, that Lowdin's symmetric orthogonalization S^{-1/2}HS^{-1/2} gives the same answer, and that enlarging the basis lowers the energy toward the exact H2+ value, as the variational principle requires.
Roothaan-Hall equations: solving HC = SCE in a finite basis

chemistrykit.HalfReaction: Days after learning of Volta's newly announced pile, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle connected one to a bowl of water in May 1800 and watched gas bubble from each wire -- the first electrolysis, and the first new discovery the pile made possible. This example reconstructs both halves of that observation from functions already in this package: the theoretical minimum decomposition voltage of water (~chemistrykit.electrochem.systems.electrolysis.minimum_applied_voltage_electrolytic, applied to the tabulated H+/H2 and O2/H2O standard potentials) comes out at the textbook 1.23 V, and Faraday's law (~chemistrykit.electrochem.systems.electrolysis.moles_from_charge) recovers the 2:1 hydrogen-to-oxygen ratio Nicholson and Carlisle actually saw bubbling from the two wires, directly from electron-transfer stoichiometry.

chemistrykit.HarmonicMolecule: Ryckaert, Ciccotti, and Berendsen's SHAKE algorithm (1977) replaces stiff bond springs by exact length constraints, restored after every Verlet position update by iterative corrections along the old bond vectors (~chemistrykit.md.systems.constraints.shake). A water-like triatomic is simulated twice: with stiff harmonic O-H springs (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicMolecule), and with the two bonds held rigid by SHAKE (~chemistrykit.md.systems.constraints.ShakeMolecule), keeping the same flexible angle-bending term. Both runs use the same time step, chosen comfortably for the slow bending motion but too long for the fast bond stretch.
SHAKE: rigid bonds let a bending molecule take larger time steps

HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A bent, water-like triatomic (one heavy vertex atom, two light outer atoms, equilibrium angle 104.5 degrees) is displaced away from its equilibrium geometry and left to vibrate under velocity-Verlet integration alone (no thermostat): both bond lengths and the bond angle oscillate indefinitely about their equilibrium values, and the total energy is conserved to within integration error.
A bent triatomic molecule: coupled bond-stretch and angle-bend vibrations

chemistrykit.HeliumVariationalResult: Helium was the first test of quantum mechanics beyond one electron. Kellner (1927) and Hylleraas (1928-1929) attacked it with the variational method: take both electrons in hydrogen-like 1s orbitals but let the nuclear charge they "see" be an adjustable \zeta. The energy E(\zeta)=(\zeta^2-2Z\zeta+\tfrac{5}{8}\zeta)E_h (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.helium.helium_like_variational_energy) is lowest at \zeta=Z-5/16=27/16 for helium (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.helium.optimize_helium_like_effective_charge): each electron shields the other from 5/16 of a nuclear charge. The result, -2.848\,E_h, is within 2% of the exact -2.9037\,E_h, which Hylleraas approached by adding the interelectronic distance to the trial function.
Kellner and Hylleraas: the variational helium atom and its screened charge

Comparing the four textbook lattices shows the close-packed pair at exactly that bound.
Kepler's conjecture: packing efficiency of SC, BCC, FCC, and HCP

chemistrykit.HuckelSystem: Erich Huckel's 1931 pi-electron theory reduces a planar conjugated ring to a small matrix eigenvalue problem: one 2p_z orbital per carbon, Coulomb integral \alpha on the diagonal, and resonance integral \beta only between bonded neighbours (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem). Filling the resulting levels two electrons at a time shows why rings with 4n+2 pi electrons (benzene, 6) form a closed shell while rings with 4n (cyclobutadiene, 4) leave two electrons unpaired in a degenerate pair. is_aromatic_by_huckel_rule checks the rule against the computed degeneracies, not only by counting electrons.
Huckel's 4n+2 aromaticity rule from the computed pi spectrum

Linus Pauling's The Nature of the Chemical Bond made "resonance energy" the chemist's measure of the extra stability a molecule gains because its true structure is a superposition of several Lewis structures (benzene's two Kekule structures foremost). In Huckel theory that stabilization is the delocalization energy (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem.delocalization_energy): the computed pi energy minus that of the same electrons held in isolated, ethylene-like double bonds, 2(\alpha+\beta) per bond.
Pauling's resonance energy as Huckel delocalization energy

Kenichi Fukui, Teijiro Yonezawa and Haruo Shingu (1952) proposed that an aromatic hydrocarbon's site of electrophilic substitution is set by one orbital alone, the highest occupied molecular orbital: the attacking electrophile goes where the HOMO density 2c_r^2 is largest. For naphthalene the Huckel HOMO has coefficient 0.425 on the alpha carbons (1, 4, 5, 8), 0.263 on the beta carbons (2, 3, 6, 7), and zero on the bridgeheads, so frontier_electron_density predicts alpha substitution, which is what nitration and halogenation mostly give.
Fukui's frontier orbitals: why naphthalene reacts at the alpha position
Charles Coulson (1939) defined the pi bond order between neighbouring atoms from the Huckel molecular orbitals themselves,
Coulson's molecular-orbital bond order in butadiene, hexatriene, and benzene

Coulson (1939) wrote the Huckel eigenvalues of a linear chain of n atoms in closed form, E_k=\alpha+2\beta\cos(k\pi/(n+1)), and Frost and Musulin (1953) turned the ring result E_k=\alpha+2\beta\cos(2\pi k/n) into a drawing: put a regular n-gon, one vertex pointing down, inside a circle of radius 2|\beta|; the heights of the vertices are the orbital energies. Flory's mean-field argument (Principles of Polymer Chemistry, 1953) predicts how excluded volume changes a chain's size scaling. IdealChain gives the exact random-walk result \langle R^2angle=nb^2. RealChain scales instead as R\sim bn^
u, with the Flory exponent 
u set by solvent quality: a good solvent swells the chain (
u\approx0.6), a poor solvent collapses it (
u=1/3), and the theta solvent reproduces the ideal chain exactly (
u=1/2).

Kuhn (1934) modeled a flexible polymer as a random walk of n freely jointed segments of length b. freely_jointed_chain samples such conformations directly; averaging their squared end-to-end distance reproduces the exact result \langle R^2\rangle=nb^2 (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_statistics.IdealChain), and the end-to-end vector's components become Gaussian with variance nb^2/3, as the central limit theorem predicts.

chemistrykit.IdealGas: Clapeyron's 1834 combined gas law unites Boyle's law (PV constant at fixed T), Charles's and Gay-Lussac's law (V \propto T at fixed P), and Avogadro's hypothesis into PV_m = RT. This example draws both classic views with IdealGas: hyperbolic Boyle isotherms, and straight Charles isobars that all extrapolate to zero volume at absolute zero.
Clapeyron's ideal gas law, PV = RT

Redlich and Kwong divided van der Waals's attraction term by \sqrt{T}. This example draws CO2 P-V isotherms well above and just below the critical temperature from RedlichKwong, with VanDerWaals and IdealGas for comparison. Both real-gas equations are built from CO2's critical temperature and pressure alone via from_critical_constants. Redlich-Kwong's universal critical compressibility factor is 1/3, closer to real gases than van der Waals's 3/8.
Redlich-Kwong isotherms of CO2 against van der Waals and the ideal gas

van't Hoff found that a dilute solution's osmotic pressure (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.osmotic_pressure) equals the pressure the solute particles would exert as an ideal gas at the same concentration and temperature. The factor i counts particles per formula unit: 1 for sucrose, about 2 for NaCl. The same factor multiplies the other colligative effects, freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.freezing_point_depression, boiling_point_elevation).
van't Hoff's osmotic pressure law, Pi = iMRT

chemistrykit.IdealGasMolecule: James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"

chemistrykit.Ising1D: Ernst Ising (1925) solved the chain of spins s_i=\pm1 with nearest-neighbor coupling J and found no spontaneous magnetization at any temperature above zero. Ising1D solves it with the 2x2 transfer matrix, whose eigenvalues \lambda_\pm give Z_N=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N exactly. The plots show a checked partition function, a magnetization that is a smooth function of field at every temperature (it only becomes a step at T=0), a correlation length that grows as e^{2J/k_BT} but stays finite, and a smooth heat-capacity maximum instead of a singularity.
Ising's one-dimensional chain: no phase transition

chemistrykit.Ising2DOnsager: Onsager (1944) computed the free energy of the square-lattice Ising model exactly: the first exact solution of a model with a genuine phase transition. Ising2DOnsager evaluates his free energy, internal energy, and heat capacity, together with Yang's (1952) spontaneous magnetization m=[1-\sinh^{-4}(2J/k_BT)]^{1/8}. The heat capacity diverges logarithmically at T_c, and the magnetization vanishes with exponent \beta=1/8. Neither the mean-field (Bragg-Williams) theory, shown for comparison, nor Ising's own one-dimensional chain reproduces these features.

chemistrykit.KapustinskiiLatticeEnergy: Kapustinskii (1956) replaced the structure-specific Madelung constant with a near-universal constant per ion, so KapustinskiiLatticeEnergy needs only the number of ions per formula unit, the charges, and the ionic radii. On rock-salt halides it tracks the structure-based Born-Lande value; it also handles salts of other structures (fluorite CaF2) where no Madelung constant is supplied at all.
Kapustinskii equation: lattice energy without a crystal structure
chemistrykit.KineticsResult: Michaelis and Menten (1913) showed that an enzyme-catalyzed rate saturates with substrate, v = V_{max}[S]/(K_m + [S]), reaching exactly half of V_{max} at [S] = K_m. This example draws that saturation curve with its two limiting regimes, integrates the substrate-depletion progress curve an assay actually records, and shows how competitive and noncompetitive inhibitors distort the curve.
Michaelis and Menten's saturating enzyme rate law
Bodenstein (1913) set the net rate of change of a short-lived intermediate to zero; Lindemann (1922) used exactly that trick on the energized molecule A^* of the mechanism
Bodenstein's steady-state approximation and Lindemann's unimolecular fall-off

StoichiometricNetwork's general mass-action engine, applied to a three-step radical chain mechanism (initiation, branching propagation, and linear termination), reproduces the qualitative signature of a chain-branching explosion: below a critical branching rate the radical concentration stays small and the fuel decays gently, while above it the radical population grows explosively and burns through the fuel in a short, sharp spike -- exactly the ignition-vs-no-ignition switch behind Semenov's and Hinshelwood's explosion-limit theory.
Chain-branching explosions and Semenov's critical condition
Bateman (1910) solved the chain of first-order steps A \xrightarrow{k_1} B \xrightarrow{k_2} C (written for radioactive decay series, but identical for consecutive chemical reactions) in closed form:
Bateman's closed-form solution for consecutive reactions

Eigen (1954) measured reactions far too fast to mix by perturbing an equilibrium mixture (a sudden temperature, pressure, or field jump) and timing its exponential return to the new equilibrium. For A \rightleftharpoons B the relaxation time is \tau = 1/(k_f + k_r), so combining \tau with the equilibrium constant K = k_f/k_r yields both rate constants. For the association A + B \rightleftharpoons C linearizing about equilibrium gives 1/\tau = k_f([A]_{eq} + [B]_{eq}) + k_r, the formula Eigen used to show that H^+ + OH^- recombination is diffusion-controlled.
Eigen's chemical relaxation: temperature jump and relaxation time

For two competing channels A \xrightarrow{k_1} B and A \xrightarrow{k_2} C, the reactant decays with the sum k_1 + k_2, while the product ratio [B]/[C] = k_1/k_2 is fixed at every instant -- the kinetic basis of product selectivity. Integrated with parallel.

Below the Hopf-bifurcation threshold (:math:`B < 1 + A^2`) the Brusselator's single fixed point is a stable focus and any initial concentration relaxes toward it. Above threshold, that same fixed point becomes unstable and every trajectory is drawn instead onto a surrounding stable limit cycle -- sustained chemical oscillation with no external forcing, driven purely by the autocatalytic X^2 Y term.
Prigogine and Lefever's Brusselator limit cycle
Lotka's 1920 chemical scheme, with the reservoir A held constant,
Lotka's autocatalytic oscillator and its neutral orbits

Field and Noyes (1974) boiled the FKN mechanism of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction -- cerium-catalyzed oxidation of malonic acid by bromate -- down to three intermediates: HBrO\ 2 (x), bromide (y), and the oxidized catalyst Ce(IV) (z). The resulting "Oregonator" (~chemistrykit.kinetics.systems.oscillators.Oregonator) produces the BZ reaction's hallmark relaxation oscillations: long quiet stretches while bromide is slowly consumed, then an autocatalytic burst of HBrO\ 2 that oxidizes the catalyst (the colour flash seen by Belousov), which in turn regenerates bromide and shuts the burst off. Raising the stoichiometric factor f well above 2 stabilizes the steady state and the oscillation disappears.
The Oregonator: oscillations of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction

Bodenstein (1913) measured that one absorbed photon forms up to 10^5-10^6 HCl molecules in an illuminated H2/Cl2 mixture, apparently violating photochemical equivalence. Nernst (1918) explained it: the photon only splits one Cl2 into two Cl atoms, which then start a chain (Cl + H2 -> HCl + H, H + Cl2 -> HCl + Cl) that runs until two atoms recombine. hydrogen_chlorine_chain_network integrates this mechanism, and chain_quantum_yield gives the steady-state yield \Phi=2k_2[\mathrm{H_2}]/\sqrt{k_t I_{abs}}. Rate constants are in arbitrary consistent units.
Bodenstein and Nernst: the H2 + Cl2 photochemical chain reaction

jablonski_network builds the 3-state (S1, T1, S0) Jablonski excited-state decay network as a StoichiometricNetwork -- reusing the kinetics domain's general mass-action reaction-network engine rather than reimplementing rate-equation integration. The numerical integration is checked here against jablonski_populations_analytic's closed-form solution.

A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.
Flory's steady-state kinetics of free-radical polymerization

free_radical_network's mode argument selects between the two ways two growing radical chains can terminate: combination (they fuse into a single dead chain) or disproportionation (one radical abstracts a hydrogen from the other, producing two separate dead chains). Bevington, Melville, and Taylor ("The Termination Reaction in Radical Polymerizations," J. Polym. Sci. 12 (1954), 449-459) showed how to distinguish the two experimentally, by end-group analysis and by the resulting degree of polymerization's relationship to the kinetic chain length (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.kinetic_chain_length) nu: \bar X_n = 2\nu for combination (two radicals' worth of monomer per dead chain) but \bar X_n = \nu for disproportionation (one radical's worth per dead chain) -- verified here directly against the numerically integrated network.

chemistrykit.KohlrauschFit: Kohlrausch found that the molar conductivity of a strong electrolyte falls linearly with \sqrt{c}, \Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - K\sqrt{c}, and that the infinite-dilution value \Lambda_m^\circ is a sum of independent ionic contributions. This example extrapolates noisy KCl data to infinite dilution with fit_kohlrausch_law, and uses limiting_molar_conductivity for his classic trick: the limiting conductivity of the weak acid acetic acid, which cannot be extrapolated, from three strong electrolytes.
Kohlrausch's laws: independent migration and the square-root law
chemistrykit.LJFluid: Rahman's 1964 simulation followed 864 argon atoms interacting through a Lennard-Jones potential with \epsilon/k_B = 120\ \text{K} and \sigma = 3.4\ \text{\AA}, at T = 94.4\ \text{K} and a mass density of 1.374\ \text{g/cm}^3 -- liquid argon just above its triple point. Here the same state point is simulated with LJFluid (512 atoms, reduced units), and the radial distribution function (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid.radial_distribution_function) is converted back to ångströms, as Rahman compared it with neutron- and X-ray-scattering data on real liquid argon.
Rahman's liquid argon: g(r) of a Lennard-Jones liquid in real units

A direct link between chemistrykit.md and chemistrykit.statmech: molecular dynamics produces an actual ensemble of particle velocities, and statistical mechanics predicts what their distribution should look like at equilibrium. After a short equilibration run, an LJFluid's particle speeds are histogrammed and compared against chemistrykit.statmech.MaxwellBoltzmannSpeedDistribution evaluated at the simulation's own (instantaneous, measured) temperature -- no fitting involved.
Cross-checking an MD trajectory against the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution

Alder and Wainwright's 1957 computer experiments showed that particles with no attraction at all -- hard spheres -- order into a crystal-like arrangement once they are packed densely enough: freezing driven by excluded volume (entropy), not by energy. This package integrates smooth forces rather than hard-sphere collision events, so the hard spheres are approximated by steeply repulsive particles: the Lennard-Jones potential cut off at its own minimum r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min) and shifted, which leaves only a repulsive wall. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low density and at a density near hard-sphere freezing shows sharp positional order appearing from packing alone.
Alder and Wainwright's hard spheres: packing-driven order with no attraction
Weeks, Chandler, and Andersen split the Lennard-Jones potential at its minimum r_m=2^{1/6}\sigma into a purely repulsive reference part u_0 and a smooth attractive perturbation w:
Weeks-Chandler-Andersen: repulsive forces set the structure of a dense liquid
Verlet's 1967 algorithm advances positions from the two previous positions and the current force,
Verlet's integrator: bounded energy error instead of drift

Checking every pair of N particles costs N(N-1)/2 distance evaluations per step. Verlet's 1967 trick: list the pairs within r_c + r_\text{skin} and reuse that list for several steps; a pair outside the list can only come inside the true cutoff r_c after the two particles have closed the skin distance between them. VerletNeighborList implements this. Here a Lennard-Jones fluid is run with a list that is never rebuilt, and at every step the listed pairs are checked against the exact set of pairs inside the cutoff (~chemistrykit.md.utils.neighbor_list.build_neighbor_list), for lists built with no skin and with a skin of 0.3\sigma.
Verlet's neighbor list: a skin that lets one pair list serve many steps

Einstein's 1905 analysis of Brownian motion showed that a particle performing a random walk wanders off, on average, not in proportion to time but to its square root: the mean-squared displacement grows linearly,
Einstein's diffusion law: mean-squared displacement grows linearly in time

Green-Kubo: the diffusion coefficient as the integral of the velocity autocorrelation

Here a Lennard-Jones fluid is run with a list that is never rebuilt, and at every step the listed pairs are checked against the exact set of pairs inside the cutoff (~chemistrykit.md.utils.neighbor_list.build_neighbor_list), for lists built with no skin and with a skin of 0.3\sigma.
Verlet's neighbor list: a skin that lets one pair list serve many steps

chemistrykit.LangmuirFit: LangmuirIsotherm models monolayer adsorption on a fixed pool of identical surface sites. Its fractional coverage \theta=KP/(1+KP) reaches exactly one-half at the half-saturation pressure P=1/K, and fit_langmuir recovers (K, qmax) from noisy loading-vs-pressure data via the standard 1/q-vs-1/P linearization.
chemistrykit.LangmuirIsotherm: Balandin's multiplet theory (1929) predicted that when catalytic activity is plotted against binding strength across a series of catalysts, it rises, peaks and falls again, tracing a "volcano". Bligaard, Norskov and coworkers (2004) later derived that shape from the Bronsted-Evans-Polanyi relation. This example reproduces the volcano with the standard textbook toy model (Chorkendorff & Niemantsverdriet, Concepts of Modern Catalysis and Kinetics, 2nd ed., Wiley-VCH, 2007, Ch. 8). The rate needs an occupied site to hold the intermediate and an empty site for the next step, so rate \propto\theta(1-\theta), with \theta the Langmuir coverage (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.langmuir.langmuir_coverage). The adsorption constant K stands in for binding strength. A hypothetical series of catalysts sits on the two legs of the volcano, and its summit is exactly Langmuir's half-saturation point K = 1/P. This is not a literal reproduction of Balandin's multiplet equations.
Balandin's volcano curve: catalytic activity peaks at intermediate binding

chemistrykit.LatticeEnergyModel: Born and Lande (1918) balanced the Madelung attraction -A/r against a short-range repulsion B/r^n; setting dU/dr=0 at the observed spacing r_0 gives U=-\frac{N_AM|z_+z_-|e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0}(1-\frac{1}{n}), which BornLandeLatticeEnergy evaluates. This example shows the energy curve for NaCl and compares the equation with Born-Haber values for six rock-salt halides.
Born-Lande equation: lattice energies of the alkali halides

Kapustinskii (1956) replaced the structure-specific Madelung constant with a near-universal constant per ion, so KapustinskiiLatticeEnergy needs only the number of ions per formula unit, the charges, and the ionic radii. On rock-salt halides it tracks the structure-based Born-Lande value; it also handles salts of other structures (fluorite CaF2) where no Madelung constant is supplied at all.

chemistrykit.LennardJones: Alder and Wainwright's 1957 computer experiments showed that particles with no attraction at all -- hard spheres -- order into a crystal-like arrangement once they are packed densely enough: freezing driven by excluded volume (entropy), not by energy. This package integrates smooth forces rather than hard-sphere collision events, so the hard spheres are approximated by steeply repulsive particles: the Lennard-Jones potential cut off at its own minimum r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min) and shifted, which leaves only a repulsive wall. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low density and at a density near hard-sphere freezing shows sharp positional order appearing from packing alone.
Alder and Wainwright's hard spheres: packing-driven order with no attraction
Weeks, Chandler, and Andersen split the Lennard-Jones potential at its minimum r_m=2^{1/6}\sigma into a purely repulsive reference part u_0 and a smooth attractive perturbation w:
Weeks-Chandler-Andersen: repulsive forces set the structure of a dense liquid

The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

chemistrykit.LewisStructure: G. N. Lewis (1916) described a covalent bond as a pair of electrons shared by two atoms, and each atom as seeking an octet of eight valence electrons. Often several octet-satisfying structures can be drawn for one molecule. Formal charge ranks them: split every bonding pair evenly, count the electrons each atom then owns, and compare with the free atom,
Lewis's shared electron pair: choosing between Lewis structures by formal charge

Walther Kossel (1916) described bonding as the complete transfer of electrons from one atom to another, leaving ions with noble-gas configurations held together by electrostatic attraction. Oxidation states are the bookkeeping version of that picture: give every bonding pair entirely to the more electronegative atom (sharing only between identical atoms) and compare the electron count with the free atom.
Kossel's ionic bond: oxidation states as the fully ionic limit

chemistrykit.LinearCalibration: The method of least squares picks the straight line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals S(m,b)=\sum_i(y_i-mx_i-b)^2. fit_calibration performs exactly that fit for a set of calibration standards; here we check that its slope sits at the bottom of the S(m) parabola, and that the residuals it leaves behind scatter around zero.
Legendre and Gauss's least squares: fitting a calibration line

Long and Winefordner argued that a detection limit should be tied to the calibration's own residual scatter s_{y/x} and slope m. lod and loq use the widely adopted calibration-based convention \text{LOD}=3.3\,s_{y/x}/m and \text{LOQ}=10\,s_{y/x}/m. A noisier method has proportionally higher limits.

chemistrykit.MargulesSolution: Margules wrote the activity coefficients of a binary liquid as power series in mole fraction. The one-parameter form used by MargulesSolution, \ln\gamma_1 = A x_2^2 and \ln\gamma_2 = A x_1^2, turns Raoult's straight lines into curves: A > 0 (unlike molecules repel) bows the total pressure upward and can produce a maximum-pressure azeotrope, while A < 0 bows it downward. The model still obeys the Gibbs-Duhem relation, and each component tends to Henry's law at infinite dilution.

Otto Stern's 1920 molecular-beam apparatus gave the first direct experimental measurement of a gas's actual molecular speeds, rather than only their statistical consequences (pressure, diffusion, viscosity) -- a rotating-drum time-of-flight technique later refined by Zartman and Ko (1930-1934) into a quantitative confirmation of the full Maxwell-Boltzmann functional form, not just its mean. sample draws exactly such a synthetic "beam" of molecular speeds; binning it into a histogram and comparing it to the exact analytic pdf reproduces the kind of check Stern, and later Zartman and Ko, made directly against a real gas.
Verifying the speed distribution: Stern's molecular-beam experiment

chemistrykit.MichaelisMentenFit: Lineweaver and Burk (1934) inverted the Michaelis-Menten equation into a straight line, 1/v = (K_m/V_{max})(1/[S]) + 1/V_{max}, so V_{max} and K_m could be read off the intercept and slope. fit_lineweaver_burk does exactly that fit on noisy initial-rate data. The second panel shows the method's well-known weakness: the same small relative noise becomes a large scatter at the low-[S] (large 1/[S]) end, which dominates the fitted line.
chemistrykit.MichaelisMentenProgress: Michaelis and Menten (1913) showed that an enzyme-catalyzed rate saturates with substrate, v = V_{max}[S]/(K_m + [S]), reaching exactly half of V_{max} at [S] = K_m. This example draws that saturation curve with its two limiting regimes, integrates the substrate-depletion progress curve an assay actually records, and shows how competitive and noncompetitive inhibitors distort the curve.
Michaelis and Menten's saturating enzyme rate law

chemistrykit.MolecularDynamicsSystem: Ryckaert, Ciccotti, and Berendsen's SHAKE algorithm (1977) replaces stiff bond springs by exact length constraints, restored after every Verlet position update by iterative corrections along the old bond vectors (~chemistrykit.md.systems.constraints.shake). A water-like triatomic is simulated twice: with stiff harmonic O-H springs (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicMolecule), and with the two bonds held rigid by SHAKE (~chemistrykit.md.systems.constraints.ShakeMolecule), keeping the same flexible angle-bending term. Both runs use the same time step, chosen comfortably for the slow bending motion but too long for the fast bond stretch.
SHAKE: rigid bonds let a bending molecule take larger time steps

The harmonic bond potential (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) is the small-oscillation limit of the anharmonic Morse potential -- they agree near the equilibrium separation but diverge away from it (Morse correctly flattens out toward a finite dissociation energy; harmonic does not). DiatomicOscillator integrates the classical two-body bond-vibration problem via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator, for either potential.
Morse vs. harmonic bond potentials, and diatomic bond vibration

HarmonicMolecule builds a small molecular-mechanics "force field" out of nothing but harmonic bond (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) and harmonic angle-bend (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicAngle) terms -- the classical, spring-and-hinge picture of molecular structure that founded molecular mechanics. A bent, water-like triatomic (one heavy vertex atom, two light outer atoms, equilibrium angle 104.5 degrees) is displaced away from its equilibrium geometry and left to vibrate under velocity-Verlet integration alone (no thermostat): both bond lengths and the bond angle oscillate indefinitely about their equilibrium values, and the total energy is conserved to within integration error.
A bent triatomic molecule: coupled bond-stretch and angle-bend vibrations

A direct link between chemistrykit.md and chemistrykit.statmech: molecular dynamics produces an actual ensemble of particle velocities, and statistical mechanics predicts what their distribution should look like at equilibrium. After a short equilibration run, an LJFluid's particle speeds are histogrammed and compared against chemistrykit.statmech.MaxwellBoltzmannSpeedDistribution evaluated at the simulation's own (instantaneous, measured) temperature -- no fitting involved.
Cross-checking an MD trajectory against the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution

Alder and Wainwright's 1957 computer experiments showed that particles with no attraction at all -- hard spheres -- order into a crystal-like arrangement once they are packed densely enough: freezing driven by excluded volume (entropy), not by energy. This package integrates smooth forces rather than hard-sphere collision events, so the hard spheres are approximated by steeply repulsive particles: the Lennard-Jones potential cut off at its own minimum r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min) and shifted, which leaves only a repulsive wall. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low density and at a density near hard-sphere freezing shows sharp positional order appearing from packing alone.
Alder and Wainwright's hard spheres: packing-driven order with no attraction
Weeks, Chandler, and Andersen split the Lennard-Jones potential at its minimum r_m=2^{1/6}\sigma into a purely repulsive reference part u_0 and a smooth attractive perturbation w:
Weeks-Chandler-Andersen: repulsive forces set the structure of a dense liquid
Verlet's 1967 algorithm advances positions from the two previous positions and the current force,
Verlet's integrator: bounded energy error instead of drift

Checking every pair of N particles costs N(N-1)/2 distance evaluations per step. Verlet's 1967 trick: list the pairs within r_c + r_\text{skin} and reuse that list for several steps; a pair outside the list can only come inside the true cutoff r_c after the two particles have closed the skin distance between them. VerletNeighborList implements this. Here a Lennard-Jones fluid is run with a list that is never rebuilt, and at every step the listed pairs are checked against the exact set of pairs inside the cutoff (~chemistrykit.md.utils.neighbor_list.build_neighbor_list), for lists built with no skin and with a skin of 0.3\sigma.
Verlet's neighbor list: a skin that lets one pair list serve many steps

chemistrykit.Molecule: Peter Debye (1912) explained why some gases have a dielectric constant that falls with temperature: their molecules carry a permanent electric dipole moment \boldsymbol\mu = \sum_i q_i \mathbf r_i, which thermal motion partly disorders. The measured moment tests a proposed shape. Water's 1.85 D rules out a linear H-O-H, while carbon dioxide's zero moment requires a linear O=C=O.
Debye's permanent dipole moments: polar and nonpolar molecules from geometry

Arthur Schoenflies named every point group after the symmetry elements that generate it: a principal axis C_n, extra C_2 axes (D_n), mirror planes \sigma_v or \sigma_h, an inversion centre i, and the special cubic groups T_d and O_h. This example builds four molecules from their real 3D geometry, lets determine_point_group find the symmetry elements by testing the coordinates directly, and shows how the elements it finds spell out each Schoenflies symbol: C_{2v}, C_{3v}, T_d and D_{\infty h}.
Schoenflies point-group symbols for water, ammonia, methane, and carbon dioxide

In 1893 Alfred Werner proposed that a six-coordinate metal complex places its ligands at the corners of an octahedron. No experiment could see the shape directly, so he argued from isomer counts. A complex \mathrm{MA_4B_2} such as [\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2}]^+ has only two forms (green trans "praseo" and violet cis "violeo"). An octahedron gives exactly two ways to place the two B ligands; a flat hexagon or a trigonal prism gives three. For \mathrm{MA_3B_3} the octahedron again gives two (fac and mer).
Werner's coordination theory: counting isomers to prove the octahedron

Adolf von Baeyer (1885) combined van't Hoff's tetrahedral carbon with the assumption that rings are flat. A planar ring of n carbons has interior angles 180^\circ(n-2)/n, so each bond must bend away from the tetrahedral 109.47 degrees by
Baeyer's strain theory: angle strain in planar cycloalkane rings

Builds four molecules spanning the five idealized electron-domain polyhedra -- methane (AX4E0, tetrahedral), water (AX2E2, bent from a tetrahedral parent), sulfur tetrafluoride (AX4E1, seesaw from a trigonal bipyramidal parent), and xenon tetrafluoride (AX4E2, square planar from an octahedral parent) -- via build_vsepr_molecule, and verifies the exact idealized bond angles each shape predicts.
VSEPR geometry prediction: from steric number to real 3D coordinates

Jacobus van't Hoff and Joseph Le Bel independently proposed in 1874 that a carbon atom's four bonds point toward the vertices of a regular tetrahedron -- and that a carbon bonded to four different substituents therefore has no internal mirror symmetry: its mirror image cannot be superimposed on itself by any rotation, giving two distinct, non- interconvertible molecules (enantiomers). This builds a genuinely tetrahedral AX4 center -- bromochlorofluoromethane, CHFClBr, the textbook minimal chiral carbon -- from domain_positions's real 3D vertex coordinates, confirms the exact 109.47-degree bond angles van't Hoff and Le Bel's model predicts, and then demonstrates the chirality itself numerically: a scalar-triple-product handedness invariant flips sign under reflection but is exactly preserved under any proper rotation (built with rotation_matrix), so no rotation can ever turn the molecule into its own mirror image.
Van't Hoff and Le Bel's tetrahedral carbon: chirality from real 3D coordinates

James Musher (1969) grouped molecules such as \mathrm{PCl_5}, \mathrm{SF_6}, \mathrm{ClF_3} and the xenon fluorides into one class: hypervalent molecules, whose central main-group atom appears to hold more than the eight electrons of Lewis's octet. Counting the Lewis electrons around the central atom (two per bond plus two per lone pair) gives 10 or 12 for all of them.
Musher's hypervalent molecules: main-group centres beyond the octet

Predicts HCl's fundamental IR absorption from a harmonic oscillator, compares it against the exact (anharmonic) Morse-potential fundamental and first overtone, then inverts the observed 0\to1/0\to2 band positions to recover the spectroscopic constants \omega_e/\omega_ex_e -- exactly the way real anharmonicity constants are measured from an observed overtone spectrum.
Harmonic vs. Morse IR band positions, and recovering anharmonicity from overtones

chemistrykit.NormalModeResult: This example uses Wilson's GF-matrix method to calculate normal modes for a linear triatomic (CO2) and a bent one (H2O) with TriatomicNormalModes. The molecule's geometry and masses give the kinetic-energy matrix G=BM^{-1}B^T, where B is the Wilson B-matrix. A diagonal valence force field gives the potential-energy matrix F. Solving the eigenvalue problem GFL=L\Lambda, with \lambda_k=(2\pi c\tilde\nu_k)^2, gives the normal-mode wavenumbers. Changing only the bend entry of F shifts the bend frequency, while the stretches barely move.
Wilson's GF-matrix method: CO2 and H2O normal-mode frequencies from the G and F matrices

Raman and Krishnan (1928) found that a small fraction of scattered light is shifted in frequency by a molecule's vibrational wavenumbers. A mode is Raman-active if it changes the molecule's polarizability. It is infrared-active if it changes the dipole moment. For a centrosymmetric molecule such as CO2, no mode is active in both spectra.
Raman scattering vs. infrared absorption: the mutual exclusion rule for CO2

Herzberg's Infrared and Raman Spectra of Polyatomic Molecules (1945) set out the rules for counting and labelling vibrations of polyatomic molecules. A nonlinear molecule of N atoms has 3N-6 vibrations. A linear molecule has 3N-5, because rotation about its axis does not count as a degree of freedom. For CO2 this means four vibrations: the symmetric stretch, the antisymmetric stretch, and a doubly degenerate bend (in-plane and out-of-plane bending have the same frequency by cylindrical symmetry). This example compares linear CO2 with bent H2O using TriatomicNormalModes, whose is_linear flag marks the bend as a degenerate pair.
Herzberg's linear-molecule rules: CO2's doubly degenerate bend and 3N-5 vibrations

chemistrykit.Oregonator: Field and Noyes (1974) boiled the FKN mechanism of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction -- cerium-catalyzed oxidation of malonic acid by bromate -- down to three intermediates: HBrO\ 2 (x), bromide (y), and the oxidized catalyst Ce(IV) (z). The resulting "Oregonator" (~chemistrykit.kinetics.systems.oscillators.Oregonator) produces the BZ reaction's hallmark relaxation oscillations: long quiet stretches while bromide is slowly consumed, then an autocatalytic burst of HBrO\ 2 that oxidizes the catalyst (the colour flash seen by Belousov), which in turn regenerates bromide and shuts the burst off. Raising the stoichiometric factor f well above 2 stabilizes the steady state and the oscillation disappears.
The Oregonator: oscillations of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction

Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low density and at a density near hard-sphere freezing shows sharp positional order appearing from packing alone.
Alder and Wainwright's hard spheres: packing-driven order with no attraction
Weeks, Chandler, and Andersen split the Lennard-Jones potential at its minimum r_m=2^{1/6}\sigma into a purely repulsive reference part u_0 and a smooth attractive perturbation w:
Weeks-Chandler-Andersen: repulsive forces set the structure of a dense liquid

The harmonic bond potential (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicBond) is the small-oscillation limit of the anharmonic Morse potential -- they agree near the equilibrium separation but diverge away from it (Morse correctly flattens out toward a finite dissociation energy; harmonic does not). DiatomicOscillator integrates the classical two-body bond-vibration problem via the shared velocity-Verlet integrator, for either potential.
Morse vs. harmonic bond potentials, and diatomic bond vibration

The Buckingham (exp-6) potential replaces the Lennard-Jones r^{-12} repulsive wall with an exponential -- closer to the true quantum-mechanical electron-overlap repulsion -- while keeping the same r^{-6} dispersion attraction. Matched to a Lennard-Jones potential's well depth, position, and long-range tail, the two agree closely everywhere near and beyond the minimum. But the exponential repulsion is eventually overwhelmed by the unbounded -C/r^6 attractive term at short enough range, so the Buckingham potential has a second, spurious turnover well inside the true minimum: past that point it falls back toward -\infty as r\to0 instead of diverging to +\infty the way Lennard-Jones's pure r^{-12} repulsion does.
Buckingham vs. Lennard-Jones: exponential repulsion and its inner turnover

The Lennard-Jones 12-6 potential: repulsion, dispersion, and the minimum

chemistrykit.ParticleInBox1D: Plots the first few 1D particle-in-a-box wavefunctions (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.particle_in_box.ParticleInBox1D), each offset by its own energy level, then checks the textbook 3D cubic-box degeneracy pattern (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.particle_in_box.ParticleInBox3D). These are the simplest exact solutions of Schrodinger's 1926 time-independent equation -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\psi=E\psi inside hard walls: quantized energies E_n=n^2h^2/8mL^2 appear from the boundary conditions alone, with no quantization postulate.
Solving Schrodinger's equation for a particle in a box

Hans Kuhn (1949) treated the pi electrons of a linear conjugated dye as free electrons in a one-dimensional box as long as the conjugated chain. With N pi electrons filling the box levels two at a time, the lowest absorption is the HOMO to LUMO jump, \Delta E=\frac{h^2}{8mL^2}(N+1), so a longer chain (more electrons and a longer box) absorbs at longer wavelength. conjugated_dye_absorption_wavelength implements this on top of ParticleInBox1D.
Kuhn's free-electron model of conjugated dye color

chemistrykit.PartitionFunction.entropy: Gibbs (1902) showed that for a system at fixed temperature every thermodynamic function follows from the canonical partition function Q=\sum_i e^{-E_i/k_BT}:
Gibbs's canonical ensemble: all thermodynamics from one partition function
chemistrykit.PartitionFunction.from_wave: Einstein (1907) treated each vibration as a quantum oscillator of frequency \nu, so its heat capacity depends on \Theta_{\text{vib}}/T with \Theta_{\text{vib}}=h\nu/k_B. VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic's heat capacity is this formula: it vanishes as T\to0 (the vibration is "frozen out") and approaches the classical equipartition value k_B per mode only once T is comparable to \Theta_{\text{vib}}. The second plot shows why a stiff mode (like Einstein's diamond) stays frozen out at temperatures where a soft mode already behaves classically.
Einstein's quantum theory of the vibrational heat capacity

James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"

chemistrykit.PengRobinson: Peng and Robinson tuned the temperature dependence of their attraction term, \alpha(T), to Pitzer's acentric factor \omega so that the equation reproduces pure-fluid vapor pressures. This example computes the CO2 vapor-pressure curve predicted by PengRobinson (\omega = 0.224) with saturation_pressure, and compares it with van der Waals and Redlich-Kwong built from the same critical constants. Only Peng-Robinson passes through Pitzer's defining point, \log_{10}(P_{sat}/P_c) = -1 - \omega at T/T_c = 0.7.
Peng-Robinson: vapor pressures from the acentric factor

G. N. Lewis replaced pressure by the fugacity f = \phi P so that the ideal-gas form \mu = \mu^\circ + RT\ln(f/P^\circ) stays exact for real fluids. The left panel shows the fugacity coefficient \phi of supercritical CO2 computed by fugacity_coefficient from three equations of state. The right panel shows Lewis's phase-equilibrium criterion: below T_c the liquid and vapor fugacities from fugacity cross exactly at the saturation pressure.
Lewis fugacity: the effective pressure of a real gas
chemistrykit.PhotostationaryStateResult: A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

chemistrykit.PointGroupResult: Arthur Schoenflies named every point group after the symmetry elements that generate it: a principal axis C_n, extra C_2 axes (D_n), mirror planes \sigma_v or \sigma_h, an inversion centre i, and the special cubic groups T_d and O_h. This example builds four molecules from their real 3D geometry, lets determine_point_group find the symmetry elements by testing the coordinates directly, and shows how the elements it finds spell out each Schoenflies symbol: C_{2v}, C_{3v}, T_d and D_{\infty h}.
Schoenflies point-group symbols for water, ammonia, methane, and carbon dioxide

In 1893 Alfred Werner proposed that a six-coordinate metal complex places its ligands at the corners of an octahedron. No experiment could see the shape directly, so he argued from isomer counts. A complex \mathrm{MA_4B_2} such as [\mathrm{Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2}]^+ has only two forms (green trans "praseo" and violet cis "violeo"). An octahedron gives exactly two ways to place the two B ligands; a flat hexagon or a trigonal prism gives three. For \mathrm{MA_3B_3} the octahedron again gives two (fac and mer).
Werner's coordination theory: counting isomers to prove the octahedron
chemistrykit.PolymerChainModel:
Flory's mean-field argument (Principles of Polymer Chemistry, 1953) predicts how excluded volume changes a chain's size scaling. IdealChain gives the exact random-walk result \langle R^2angle=nb^2. RealChain scales instead as R\sim bn^
u, with the Flory exponent 
u set by solvent quality: a good solvent swells the chain (
u\approx0.6), a poor solvent collapses it (
u=1/3), and the theta solvent reproduces the ideal chain exactly (
u=1/2).
Flory's solvent-quality exponents: ideal vs. real chain scaling

Kuhn (1934) modeled a flexible polymer as a random walk of n freely jointed segments of length b. freely_jointed_chain samples such conformations directly; averaging their squared end-to-end distance reproduces the exact result \langle R^2\rangle=nb^2 (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_statistics.IdealChain), and the end-to-end vector's components become Gaussian with variance nb^2/3, as the central limit theorem predicts.
Kuhn's random-walk chain: sampled freely jointed chains

good_solvent uses Flory's original 1953 mean-field good-solvent exponent (
u=3/5); good_solvent_renormalization_group uses de Gennes' 1979 renormalization-group-refined value (
u\approx0.588). The two exponents differ by only about 2%, but because R\sim bn^
u is a power law, that small an exponent difference compounds with chain length: the two chain-size curves are nearly indistinguishable on a log-log plot for short chains, yet the relative difference between the predicted R values grows steadily as n increases -- exactly why precise critical exponents matter most for long-chain, asymptotic behavior.
Flory's mean-field exponent vs. the renormalization-group value

Schrodinger's first 1926 paper solved his wave equation for the hydrogen atom and recovered the Bohr energies E_n\propto-1/n^2 without any quantization postulate. HydrogenLikeAtom reproduces the textbook 13.6 eV hydrogen ground-state energy exactly, and its radial wavefunctions (built from the associated Laguerre polynomials of scipy.special) are independently checked here by numerically integrating them to a normalized probability of 1.
Schrodinger's hydrogen atom: radial wavefunctions and orbital energies

Plots the first few 1D particle-in-a-box wavefunctions (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.particle_in_box.ParticleInBox1D), each offset by its own energy level, then checks the textbook 3D cubic-box degeneracy pattern (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.particle_in_box.ParticleInBox3D). These are the simplest exact solutions of Schrodinger's 1926 time-independent equation -\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\psi=E\psi inside hard walls: quantized energies E_n=n^2h^2/8mL^2 appear from the boundary conditions alone, with no quantization postulate.
Solving Schrodinger's equation for a particle in a box

Hans Kuhn (1949) treated the pi electrons of a linear conjugated dye as free electrons in a one-dimensional box as long as the conjugated chain. With N pi electrons filling the box levels two at a time, the lowest absorption is the HOMO to LUMO jump, \Delta E=\frac{h^2}{8mL^2}(N+1), so a longer chain (more electrons and a longer box) absorbs at longer wavelength. conjugated_dye_absorption_wavelength implements this on top of ParticleInBox1D.
Kuhn's free-electron model of conjugated dye color

Predicts HCl's fundamental IR absorption from a harmonic oscillator, compares it against the exact (anharmonic) Morse-potential fundamental and first overtone, then inverts the observed 0\to1/0\to2 band positions to recover the spectroscopic constants \omega_e/\omega_ex_e -- exactly the way real anharmonicity constants are measured from an observed overtone spectrum.
Harmonic vs. Morse IR band positions, and recovering anharmonicity from overtones

Rotational lines of light molecules lie in the microwave region, which became routinely accessible after Cleeton and Williams (1934) and postwar microwave spectroscopy by Townes and others. Microwave frequencies can be measured very precisely, so isotope shifts are easy to see. Isotopic substitution leaves the bond length unchanged but changes the reduced mass, so every line of the heavier isotopologue moves down by \mu_a/\mu_b, the ratio isotope_shift_ratio predicts. This example computes the J=1\leftarrow0 lines of ^{12}\mathrm{C}^{16}\mathrm{O}, ^{13}\mathrm{C}^{16}\mathrm{O} and ^{12}\mathrm{C}^{18}\mathrm{O} in GHz and compares them with the measured values (115.271, 110.201 and 109.782 GHz).
Microwave spectroscopy and the isotope shift: CO isotopologues' J=1-0 lines in GHz

chemistrykit.RadiusRatioPrediction: Pauling's first rule (1929): each cation is surrounded by a polyhedron of anions whose size is fixed by the radius ratio r_+/r_-. A polyhedron is stable only while the anions still touch the cation, which sets the limits \sqrt2-1=0.414 (octahedral), \sqrt3-1=0.732 (cubic), and so on. radius_ratio_coordination applies the rule; here it is tested against observed structures.
Pauling's radius-ratio rule: predicting coordination numbers
chemistrykit.RateLaw: van't Hoff (1884) classified reactions by the order n of their rate law -d[A]/dt = k[A]^n. The three textbook cases -- ZeroOrder, FirstOrder, and SecondOrder -- all started from the same initial concentration and with rate constants chosen to give the same half-life, so the different curvature (linear, exponential, hyperbolic) is the only thing distinguishing them. First order is the only one whose half-life doesn't depend on the starting concentration; the plot below marks all three half-lives to make that concrete.
van't Hoff's reaction orders: zero-, first-, and second-order rate laws

Wilhelmy (1850) followed the acid-catalyzed inversion of cane sugar by polarimetry: the optical rotation \alpha(t) drifts from the dextrorotatory sucrose value towards the (levorotatory) value of the glucose + fructose mixture. Because \alpha is linear in the concentrations, \alpha(t) - \alpha_\infty is proportional to the sucrose still present, and a straight line of \ln[(\alpha - \alpha_\infty)/(\alpha_0 - \alpha_\infty)] against t identifies -d[\text{sugar}]/dt = k[\text{sugar}].
Wilhelmy's sucrose inversion: the first measured first-order rate law

chemistrykit.ReactionNetwork: Michaelis and Menten (1913) showed that an enzyme-catalyzed rate saturates with substrate, v = V_{max}[S]/(K_m + [S]), reaching exactly half of V_{max} at [S] = K_m. This example draws that saturation curve with its two limiting regimes, integrates the substrate-depletion progress curve an assay actually records, and shows how competitive and noncompetitive inhibitors distort the curve.
Michaelis and Menten's saturating enzyme rate law
Bodenstein (1913) set the net rate of change of a short-lived intermediate to zero; Lindemann (1922) used exactly that trick on the energized molecule A^* of the mechanism
Bodenstein's steady-state approximation and Lindemann's unimolecular fall-off

StoichiometricNetwork's general mass-action engine, applied to a three-step radical chain mechanism (initiation, branching propagation, and linear termination), reproduces the qualitative signature of a chain-branching explosion: below a critical branching rate the radical concentration stays small and the fuel decays gently, while above it the radical population grows explosively and burns through the fuel in a short, sharp spike -- exactly the ignition-vs-no-ignition switch behind Semenov's and Hinshelwood's explosion-limit theory.
Chain-branching explosions and Semenov's critical condition

Eigen (1954) measured reactions far too fast to mix by perturbing an equilibrium mixture (a sudden temperature, pressure, or field jump) and timing its exponential return to the new equilibrium. For A \rightleftharpoons B the relaxation time is \tau = 1/(k_f + k_r), so combining \tau with the equilibrium constant K = k_f/k_r yields both rate constants. For the association A + B \rightleftharpoons C linearizing about equilibrium gives 1/\tau = k_f([A]_{eq} + [B]_{eq}) + k_r, the formula Eigen used to show that H^+ + OH^- recombination is diffusion-controlled.
Eigen's chemical relaxation: temperature jump and relaxation time

Below the Hopf-bifurcation threshold (:math:`B < 1 + A^2`) the Brusselator's single fixed point is a stable focus and any initial concentration relaxes toward it. Above threshold, that same fixed point becomes unstable and every trajectory is drawn instead onto a surrounding stable limit cycle -- sustained chemical oscillation with no external forcing, driven purely by the autocatalytic X^2 Y term.
Prigogine and Lefever's Brusselator limit cycle
Lotka's 1920 chemical scheme, with the reservoir A held constant,
Lotka's autocatalytic oscillator and its neutral orbits

Field and Noyes (1974) boiled the FKN mechanism of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction -- cerium-catalyzed oxidation of malonic acid by bromate -- down to three intermediates: HBrO\ 2 (x), bromide (y), and the oxidized catalyst Ce(IV) (z). The resulting "Oregonator" (~chemistrykit.kinetics.systems.oscillators.Oregonator) produces the BZ reaction's hallmark relaxation oscillations: long quiet stretches while bromide is slowly consumed, then an autocatalytic burst of HBrO\ 2 that oxidizes the catalyst (the colour flash seen by Belousov), which in turn regenerates bromide and shuts the burst off. Raising the stoichiometric factor f well above 2 stabilizes the steady state and the oscillation disappears.
The Oregonator: oscillations of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction

Bodenstein (1913) measured that one absorbed photon forms up to 10^5-10^6 HCl molecules in an illuminated H2/Cl2 mixture, apparently violating photochemical equivalence. Nernst (1918) explained it: the photon only splits one Cl2 into two Cl atoms, which then start a chain (Cl + H2 -> HCl + H, H + Cl2 -> HCl + Cl) that runs until two atoms recombine. hydrogen_chlorine_chain_network integrates this mechanism, and chain_quantum_yield gives the steady-state yield \Phi=2k_2[\mathrm{H_2}]/\sqrt{k_t I_{abs}}. Rate constants are in arbitrary consistent units.
Bodenstein and Nernst: the H2 + Cl2 photochemical chain reaction

jablonski_network builds the 3-state (S1, T1, S0) Jablonski excited-state decay network as a StoichiometricNetwork -- reusing the kinetics domain's general mass-action reaction-network engine rather than reimplementing rate-equation integration. The numerical integration is checked here against jablonski_populations_analytic's closed-form solution.

A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.
Flory's steady-state kinetics of free-radical polymerization

chemistrykit.RealChain:
Flory's mean-field argument (Principles of Polymer Chemistry, 1953) predicts how excluded volume changes a chain's size scaling. IdealChain gives the exact random-walk result \langle R^2angle=nb^2. RealChain scales instead as R\sim bn^
u, with the Flory exponent 
u set by solvent quality: a good solvent swells the chain (
u\approx0.6), a poor solvent collapses it (
u=1/3), and the theta solvent reproduces the ideal chain exactly (
u=1/2).
Flory's solvent-quality exponents: ideal vs. real chain scaling

good_solvent uses Flory's original 1953 mean-field good-solvent exponent (
u=3/5); good_solvent_renormalization_group uses de Gennes' 1979 renormalization-group-refined value (
u\approx0.588). The two exponents differ by only about 2%, but because R\sim bn^
u is a power law, that small an exponent difference compounds with chain length: the two chain-size curves are nearly indistinguishable on a log-log plot for short chains, yet the relative difference between the predicted R values grows steadily as n increases -- exactly why precise critical exponents matter most for long-chain, asymptotic behavior.
Flory's mean-field exponent vs. the renormalization-group value

Dennison (1926) gave the quantum-mechanical rotational energy levels E_J=\hbar^2J(J+1)/(2I). With the \Delta J=+1 selection rule, these levels produce absorption lines at 2B(J+1), which are evenly spaced by 2B. This example builds an HCl-like rigid rotor from chemistrykit.quantum, prints its level energies and line positions, checks the constant 2B spacing, and adds the Boltzmann-population intensity pattern seen in a real far-infrared or microwave spectrum.

Rotational lines of light molecules lie in the microwave region, which became routinely accessible after Cleeton and Williams (1934) and postwar microwave spectroscopy by Townes and others. Microwave frequencies can be measured very precisely, so isotope shifts are easy to see. Isotopic substitution leaves the bond length unchanged but changes the reduced mass, so every line of the heavier isotopologue moves down by \mu_a/\mu_b, the ratio isotope_shift_ratio predicts. This example computes the J=1\leftarrow0 lines of ^{12}\mathrm{C}^{16}\mathrm{O}, ^{13}\mathrm{C}^{16}\mathrm{O} and ^{12}\mathrm{C}^{18}\mathrm{O} in GHz and compares them with the measured values (115.271, 110.201 and 109.782 GHz).

chemistrykit.RotationalPartitionFunction: James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"
