chemistrykit.SecondOrder: van't Hoff (1884) classified reactions by the order n of their rate law -d[A]/dt = k[A]^n. The three textbook cases -- ZeroOrder, FirstOrder, and SecondOrder -- all started from the same initial concentration and with rate constants chosen to give the same half-life, so the different curvature (linear, exponential, hyperbolic) is the only thing distinguishing them. chemistrykit.ShakeMolecule: Ryckaert, Ciccotti, and Berendsen's SHAKE algorithm (1977) replaces stiff bond springs by exact length constraints, restored after every Verlet position update by iterative corrections along the old bond vectors (~chemistrykit.md.systems.constraints.shake). A water-like triatomic is simulated twice: with stiff harmonic O-H springs (~chemistrykit.md.systems.pair_potentials.HarmonicMolecule), and with the two bonds held rigid by SHAKE (~chemistrykit.md.systems.constraints.ShakeMolecule), keeping the same flexible angle-bending term. Both runs use the same time step, chosen comfortably for the slow bending motion but too long for the fast bond stretch.
SHAKE: rigid bonds let a bending molecule take larger time steps

Comparing the four textbook lattices shows the close-packed pair at exactly that bound.
Kepler's conjecture: packing efficiency of SC, BCC, FCC, and HCP
chemistrykit.Spectrum: Fraunhofer (1814) found that sunlight is not a smooth rainbow but a continuum crossed by hundreds of sharp dark lines at fixed, reproducible wavelengths, and he labelled the strongest ones A to K. This example builds a sun-like continuum from Planck's law at 5800 K, removes light at the tabulated positions of Fraunhofer's lettered lines using narrow Lorentzian absorption profiles, and marks each letter above its line.
Fraunhofer's dark lines: sharp absorption lines at fixed wavelengths in the solar spectrum

Bunsen and Kirchhoff (1859-1861) vaporized salts in a nearly colourless flame and found that each element gives bright lines at its own fixed wavelengths. The top panel shows the strongest visible and near-visible resonance lines of the alkali metals they studied, including caesium's blue doublet and rubidium's red and near-infrared lines, the lines that revealed those two new elements. The bottom panel illustrates Kirchhoff's law: a cooler sodium vapour placed in front of a continuous source absorbs at exactly the wavelengths where hot sodium emits. This is what explains Fraunhofer's D lines.
Kirchhoff and Bunsen's flame spectra: bright emission lines and matching dark absorption lines

Builds a vibronic progression from the Huang-Rhys displacement parameter, verifies the Franck-Condon factors' normalization (they must sum to 1 -- the required correctness check for any Franck-Condon calculation), and shows how a larger excited-state displacement shifts the most-intense vibronic peak to higher v'.

Indirect spin-spin coupling carried through the bonding electrons (Ramsey and Purcell, 1952) splits an NMR resonance into a multiplet. The splitting is J Hz regardless of field strength. In the first-order limit, n equivalent spin-1/2 neighbours give n+1 lines with Pascal's-triangle intensities. This example simulates ethanol's -CH3 triplet and -CH2- quartet, then a doublet of triplets from two inequivalent coupling partners with different J values.
Spin-spin (J) coupling and the n+1 rule: ethanol's triplet/quartet and a doublet of triplets

Karplus (1959) used valence-bond theory to show that the three-bond (vicinal) H-C-C-H coupling constant depends on the dihedral angle \phi. It is large for eclipsed (0 degrees) and anti (180 degrees) protons and nearly zero near 90 degrees. This lets a measured ^3J report molecular conformation. This example plots Karplus's 1959 curve from karplus_coupling, reads off the axial-axial and axial-equatorial couplings of a cyclohexane chair, and shows the resulting doublet splittings.

Predicts HCl's fundamental IR absorption from a harmonic oscillator, compares it against the exact (anharmonic) Morse-potential fundamental and first overtone, then inverts the observed 0\to1/0\to2 band positions to recover the spectroscopic constants \omega_e/\omega_ex_e -- exactly the way real anharmonicity constants are measured from an observed overtone spectrum.

A mode is Raman-active if it changes the molecule's polarizability. It is infrared-active if it changes the dipole moment. For a centrosymmetric molecule such as CO2, no mode is active in both spectra.

With thousands of molecules the trajectories hug the deterministic rate-equation solution; with a handful they are visibly noisy, and the average over many runs recovers the deterministic curve.

StoichiometricNetwork's general mass-action engine, applied to a three-step radical chain mechanism (initiation, branching propagation, and linear termination), reproduces the qualitative signature of a chain-branching explosion: below a critical branching rate the radical concentration stays small and the fuel decays gently, while above it the radical population grows explosively and burns through the fuel in a short, sharp spike -- exactly the ignition-vs-no-ignition switch behind Semenov's and Hinshelwood's explosion-limit theory.
Chain-branching explosions and Semenov's critical condition
Bateman (1910) solved the chain of first-order steps A \xrightarrow{k_1} B \xrightarrow{k_2} C (written for radioactive decay series, but identical for consecutive chemical reactions) in closed form:
Bateman's closed-form solution for consecutive reactions

Eigen (1954) measured reactions far too fast to mix by perturbing an equilibrium mixture (a sudden temperature, pressure, or field jump) and timing its exponential return to the new equilibrium. For A \rightleftharpoons B the relaxation time is \tau = 1/(k_f + k_r), so combining \tau with the equilibrium constant K = k_f/k_r yields both rate constants. For the association A + B \rightleftharpoons C linearizing about equilibrium gives 1/\tau = k_f([A]_{eq} + [B]_{eq}) + k_r, the formula Eigen used to show that H^+ + OH^- recombination is diffusion-controlled.
Eigen's chemical relaxation: temperature jump and relaxation time

For two competing channels A \xrightarrow{k_1} B and A \xrightarrow{k_2} C, the reactant decays with the sum k_1 + k_2, while the product ratio [B]/[C] = k_1/k_2 is fixed at every instant -- the kinetic basis of product selectivity. Integrated with parallel.
Lotka's 1920 chemical scheme, with the reservoir A held constant,
Lotka's autocatalytic oscillator and its neutral orbits

Bodenstein (1913) measured that one absorbed photon forms up to 10^5-10^6 HCl molecules in an illuminated H2/Cl2 mixture, apparently violating photochemical equivalence. Nernst (1918) explained it: the photon only splits one Cl2 into two Cl atoms, which then start a chain (Cl + H2 -> HCl + H, H + Cl2 -> HCl + Cl) that runs until two atoms recombine. hydrogen_chlorine_chain_network integrates this mechanism, and chain_quantum_yield gives the steady-state yield \Phi=2k_2[\mathrm{H_2}]/\sqrt{k_t I_{abs}}. Rate constants are in arbitrary consistent units.

A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Flory's steady-state kinetics of free-radical polymerization

StoichiometricNetwork's general mass-action engine, applied to a three-step radical chain mechanism (initiation, branching propagation, and linear termination), reproduces the qualitative signature of a chain-branching explosion: below a critical branching rate the radical concentration stays small and the fuel decays gently, while above it the radical population grows explosively and burns through the fuel in a short, sharp spike -- exactly the ignition-vs-no-ignition switch behind Semenov's and Hinshelwood's explosion-limit theory.

Eigen (1954) measured reactions far too fast to mix by perturbing an equilibrium mixture (a sudden temperature, pressure, or field jump) and timing its exponential return to the new equilibrium. For A \rightleftharpoons B the relaxation time is \tau = 1/(k_f + k_r), so combining \tau with the equilibrium constant K = k_f/k_r yields both rate constants. For the association A + B \rightleftharpoons C linearizing about equilibrium gives 1/\tau = k_f([A]_{eq} + [B]_{eq}) + k_r, the formula Eigen used to show that H^+ + OH^- recombination is diffusion-controlled.
Eigen's chemical relaxation: temperature jump and relaxation time

For two competing channels A \xrightarrow{k_1} B and A \xrightarrow{k_2} C, the reactant decays with the sum k_1 + k_2, while the product ratio [B]/[C] = k_1/k_2 is fixed at every instant -- the kinetic basis of product selectivity. Integrated with parallel.
Lotka's 1920 chemical scheme, with the reservoir A held constant,
Lotka's autocatalytic oscillator and its neutral orbits

chemistrykit.TPDResult: In a TPD experiment a covered surface is heated at a steady rate \beta while the desorbing gas is recorded, and each binding state shows up as a peak. simulate_tpd integrates the Polanyi-Wigner rate equation to produce these spectra. Redhead (1962) turned a first-order peak temperature T_p into a desorption energy: E_d = RT_p[\ln(\nu T_p/\beta) - 3.64] (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.tpd.redhead_desorption_energy). Below, the formula is checked against the exact peak condition (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.tpd.first_order_peak_temperature). First-order peaks shift with heating rate but not with coverage, while second-order peaks move to lower temperature as the coverage rises.

This example generates noisy "measured" high-overpotential data, draws the Tafel plot, and uses fit_tafel_plot to recover the Tafel slope b and exchange current density i_0 by linear regression -- the analysis Tafel's successors still use, and compares the slope with tafel_slope's textbook ~118 mV/decade for \alpha = 0.5, n = 1.
Tafel's law: overpotential linear in log current

chemistrykit.TemkinFit: Temkin and Pyzhev (1940), modelling ammonia synthesis on iron, dropped Langmuir's single site energy. In their picture the heat of adsorption falls linearly as the surface fills, which is the same as a uniform spread of site energies of width fRT. Averaging the Langmuir coverage over that spread (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.temkin.uniform_energy_coverage) gives an isotherm that is logarithmic over a wide middle range of coverage, \theta \approx (1/f)\ln(K_{max}P), the Temkin form. A single Langmuir curve covers only about two decades of pressure, while the Temkin curve rises steadily over many. Loading data in that range is a straight line in \ln P, which fit_temkin fits.
The Temkin isotherm: a heat of adsorption that falls with coverage

chemistrykit.TitrationCurve: RedoxTitration computes the electrode potential during a redox titration from the Nernst equation, E=E^\circ-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q: before equivalence the analyte couple sets E, after it the titrant couple does. At half-equivalence E=E^\circ_1 exactly, at twice the equivalence volume E=E^\circ_2, and the endpoint is read, as in the laboratory, at the steepest rise of E.
The Nernst equation in a potentiometric redox titration

EDTATitration follows M+Y\rightleftharpoons MY through its conditional formation constant K_f'. The same EDTA titrant quantifies any metal it binds strongly enough; the size of the pM break at equivalence is set by K_f', which is why Schwarzenbach's titrations are run in a buffer at a pH where K_f' is large.
EDTA complexometric titration of a metal ion

chemistrykit.TriatomicNormalModes: This example uses Wilson's GF-matrix method to calculate normal modes for a linear triatomic (CO2) and a bent one (H2O) with TriatomicNormalModes. The molecule's geometry and masses give the kinetic-energy matrix G=BM^{-1}B^T, where B is the Wilson B-matrix. A diagonal valence force field gives the potential-energy matrix F. Solving the eigenvalue problem GFL=L\Lambda, with \lambda_k=(2\pi c\tilde\nu_k)^2, gives the normal-mode wavenumbers. Changing only the bend entry of F shifts the bend frequency, while the stretches barely move.
Wilson's GF-matrix method: CO2 and H2O normal-mode frequencies from the G and F matrices

Raman and Krishnan (1928) found that a small fraction of scattered light is shifted in frequency by a molecule's vibrational wavenumbers. A mode is Raman-active if it changes the molecule's polarizability. It is infrared-active if it changes the dipole moment. For a centrosymmetric molecule such as CO2, no mode is active in both spectra.
Raman scattering vs. infrared absorption: the mutual exclusion rule for CO2

Herzberg's Infrared and Raman Spectra of Polyatomic Molecules (1945) set out the rules for counting and labelling vibrations of polyatomic molecules. A nonlinear molecule of N atoms has 3N-6 vibrations. A linear molecule has 3N-5, because rotation about its axis does not count as a degree of freedom. For CO2 this means four vibrations: the symmetric stretch, the antisymmetric stretch, and a doubly degenerate bend (in-plane and out-of-plane bending have the same frequency by cylindrical symmetry). This example compares linear CO2 with bent H2O using TriatomicNormalModes, whose is_linear flag marks the bend as a degenerate pair.
Herzberg's linear-molecule rules: CO2's doubly degenerate bend and 3N-5 vibrations

chemistrykit.VSEPRGeometry: Builds four molecules spanning the five idealized electron-domain polyhedra -- methane (AX4E0, tetrahedral), water (AX2E2, bent from a tetrahedral parent), sulfur tetrafluoride (AX4E1, seesaw from a trigonal bipyramidal parent), and xenon tetrafluoride (AX4E2, square planar from an octahedral parent) -- via build_vsepr_molecule, and verifies the exact idealized bond angles each shape predicts.
VSEPR geometry prediction: from steric number to real 3D coordinates

James Musher (1969) grouped molecules such as \mathrm{PCl_5}, \mathrm{SF_6}, \mathrm{ClF_3} and the xenon fluorides into one class: hypervalent molecules, whose central main-group atom appears to hold more than the eight electrons of Lewis's octet. Counting the Lewis electrons around the central atom (two per bond plus two per lone pair) gives 10 or 12 for all of them.
Musher's hypervalent molecules: main-group centres beyond the octet
chemistrykit.VanDerWaals: Andrews's CO2 isotherms showed a flat liquid-vapor plateau below a critical temperature and none above it. The van der Waals equation (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.equations_of_state.VanDerWaals), built from CO2's critical constants with from_critical_constants, reproduces the whole family: loops with three volume roots below T_c, an inflection at T_c, and single-valued isotherms above it, so gas can be turned into liquid continuously by going around the critical point.
Andrews and van der Waals: continuity of the liquid and gas states

Redlich and Kwong divided van der Waals's attraction term by \sqrt{T}. This example draws CO2 P-V isotherms well above and just below the critical temperature from RedlichKwong, with VanDerWaals and IdealGas for comparison. Both real-gas equations are built from CO2's critical temperature and pressure alone via from_critical_constants. Redlich-Kwong's universal critical compressibility factor is 1/3, closer to real gases than van der Waals's 3/8.
Redlich-Kwong isotherms of CO2 against van der Waals and the ideal gas

Peng and Robinson tuned the temperature dependence of their attraction term, \alpha(T), to Pitzer's acentric factor \omega so that the equation reproduces pure-fluid vapor pressures. This example computes the CO2 vapor-pressure curve predicted by PengRobinson (\omega = 0.224) with saturation_pressure, and compares it with van der Waals and Redlich-Kwong built from the same critical constants. Only Peng-Robinson passes through Pitzer's defining point, \log_{10}(P_{sat}/P_c) = -1 - \omega at T/T_c = 0.7.
Peng-Robinson: vapor pressures from the acentric factor

G. N. Lewis replaced pressure by the fugacity f = \phi P so that the ideal-gas form \mu = \mu^\circ + RT\ln(f/P^\circ) stays exact for real fluids. The left panel shows the fugacity coefficient \phi of supercritical CO2 computed by fugacity_coefficient from three equations of state. The right panel shows Lewis's phase-equilibrium criterion: below T_c the liquid and vapor fugacities from fugacity cross exactly at the saturation pressure.
Lewis fugacity: the effective pressure of a real gas

chemistrykit.VantHoffFit: van't Hoff's equation d\ln K/dT = \Delta H^\circ/(RT^2) makes \ln K a straight line in 1/T with slope -\Delta H^\circ/R and intercept \Delta S^\circ/R. This example generates noisy equilibrium constants for N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 from van_t_hoff_equilibrium_constant and recovers the reaction enthalpy and entropy with fit_van_t_hoff.
The van't Hoff plot: ln K against 1/T
chemistrykit.VantHoffFit.predict: van't Hoff's equation d\ln K/dT = \Delta H^\circ/(RT^2) makes \ln K a straight line in 1/T with slope -\Delta H^\circ/R and intercept \Delta S^\circ/R. This example generates noisy equilibrium constants for N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 from van_t_hoff_equilibrium_constant and recovers the reaction enthalpy and entropy with fit_van_t_hoff.
The van't Hoff plot: ln K against 1/T
chemistrykit.VariationalSolver: Hund and Mulliken's molecular-orbital theory builds one-electron orbitals spread over the whole molecule as a linear combination of atomic orbitals, \psi_\pm=c_A\chi_A\pm c_B\chi_B. H2PlusVariational does this for H2+ with one Gaussian orbital per proton: diagonalizing the 2x2 problem gives the in-phase bonding orbital (equal coefficients, energy below the isolated-atom level) and the out-of-phase antibonding orbital (opposite coefficients, energy above it). Following both orbital energies from short bond lengths out to separated atoms gives Mulliken's correlation diagram for the simplest molecule.
Hund-Mulliken LCAO molecular orbitals of H2+: bonding and antibonding

Walter Heitler and Fritz London's 1927 quantum-mechanical treatment of H2 -- the paper usually credited with founding quantum chemistry as a field -- showed for the first time why two hydrogen atoms bind: the symmetric (in-phase) combination of their two atomic orbitals builds up electron density in the region between the nuclei, lowering the energy below that of the separated atoms, while the antisymmetric (out-of-phase) combination depletes density there and raises the energy instead. Their original calculation used two-electron integrals this package does not implement (chemistrykit.quantum.utils.basis_sets stops at the one-electron integrals H2PlusVariational needs for H2+), but the same qualitative physics -- constructive vs. destructive interference of atomic orbitals along the bond axis -- is exactly what H2+'s own bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals show, using the genuine LCAO coefficients solve computes, not an assumed equal-weight combination.
Heitler-London's insight: bonding vs. antibonding electron density

Born and Oppenheimer separated the fast electrons from the slow nuclei: first solve the electronic problem with the nuclei clamped at a fixed separation R, then let the nuclei move on the resulting potential energy curve U(R)=E_{el}(R)+e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0R. Here each point of the curve is a separate clamped-nuclei calculation with H2PlusVariational (``bond_length`` is a fixed input, never a dynamical variable). The curvature at the minimum then gives a nuclear vibrational frequency, and because the electronic curve does not depend on nuclear mass, H2+ and D2+ share the same curve but have different zero-point energies.
Born-Oppenheimer clamped-nuclei potential curve of H2+

G. N. Lewis's 1916 covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. In molecular-orbital language that pair is two electrons of opposite spin in the same bonding orbital. Using the two orbitals of a hydrogen-like diatomic from H2PlusVariational (at the H2 bond length, electron-electron repulsion neglected), fill them with 1 to 4 electrons: the bond order (n_{bonding}-n_{antibonding})/2 is 1 exactly when a single Lewis pair sits in the bonding orbital, and adding a second pair to the antibonding orbital cancels the bond (the He2 case).
Lewis's shared electron pair: two opposite-spin electrons in one bonding orbital

Kenichi Fukui, Teijiro Yonezawa and Haruo Shingu (1952) proposed that an aromatic hydrocarbon's site of electrophilic substitution is set by one orbital alone, the highest occupied molecular orbital: the attacking electrophile goes where the HOMO density 2c_r^2 is largest. For naphthalene the Huckel HOMO has coefficient 0.425 on the alpha carbons (1, 4, 5, 8), 0.263 on the beta carbons (2, 3, 6, 7), and zero on the bridgeheads, so frontier_electron_density predicts alpha substitution, which is what nitration and halogenation mostly give.
Fukui's frontier orbitals: why naphthalene reacts at the alpha position
chemistrykit.VariationalSolver.cyclic_po: Erich Huckel's 1931 pi-electron theory reduces a planar conjugated ring to a small matrix eigenvalue problem: one 2p_z orbital per carbon, Coulomb integral \alpha on the diagonal, and resonance integral \beta only between bonded neighbours (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem). Filling the resulting levels two electrons at a time shows why rings with 4n+2 pi electrons (benzene, 6) form a closed shell while rings with 4n (cyclobutadiene, 4) leave two electrons unpaired in a degenerate pair. is_aromatic_by_huckel_rule checks the rule against the computed degeneracies, not only by counting electrons.
Huckel's 4n+2 aromaticity rule from the computed pi spectrum

Linus Pauling's The Nature of the Chemical Bond made "resonance energy" the chemist's measure of the extra stability a molecule gains because its true structure is a superposition of several Lewis structures (benzene's two Kekule structures foremost). In Huckel theory that stabilization is the delocalization energy (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.HuckelSystem.delocalization_energy): the computed pi energy minus that of the same electrons held in isolated, ethylene-like double bonds, 2(\alpha+\beta) per bond.
Pauling's resonance energy as Huckel delocalization energy

Coulson (1939) wrote the Huckel eigenvalues of a linear chain of n atoms in closed form, E_k=\alpha+2\beta\cos(k\pi/(n+1)), and Frost and Musulin (1953) turned the ring result E_k=\alpha+2\beta\cos(2\pi k/n) into a drawing: put a regular n-gon, one vertex pointing down, inside a circle of radius 2|\beta|; the heights of the vertices are the orbital energies. Both closed forms (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.huckel.linear_polyene_eigenvalues, cyclic_polyene_eigenvalues) are checked here against numerical diagonalization.
Coulson's polyene formula and the Frost circle
Charles Coulson (1939) defined the pi bond order between neighbouring atoms from the Huckel molecular orbitals themselves,
Coulson's molecular-orbital bond order in butadiene, hexatriene, and benzene

chemistrykit.VelocityRescalingThermostat: Rahman's 1964 simulation followed 864 argon atoms interacting through a Lennard-Jones potential with \epsilon/k_B = 120\ \text{K} and \sigma = 3.4\ \text{\AA}, at T = 94.4\ \text{K} and a mass density of 1.374\ \text{g/cm}^3 -- liquid argon just above its triple point. Here the same state point is simulated with LJFluid (512 atoms, reduced units), and the radial distribution function (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid.radial_distribution_function) is converted back to ångströms, as Rahman compared it with neutron- and X-ray-scattering data on real liquid argon.
Rahman's liquid argon: g(r) of a Lennard-Jones liquid in real units

Alder and Wainwright's 1957 computer experiments showed that particles with no attraction at all -- hard spheres -- order into a crystal-like arrangement once they are packed densely enough: freezing driven by excluded volume (entropy), not by energy. This package integrates smooth forces rather than hard-sphere collision events, so the hard spheres are approximated by steeply repulsive particles: the Lennard-Jones potential cut off at its own minimum r=2^{1/6}\sigma (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LennardJones.r_min) and shifted, which leaves only a repulsive wall. Comparing the radial distribution function g(r) of this purely repulsive LJFluid at low density and at a density near hard-sphere freezing shows sharp positional order appearing from packing alone.
Alder and Wainwright's hard spheres: packing-driven order with no attraction
Weeks, Chandler, and Andersen split the Lennard-Jones potential at its minimum r_m=2^{1/6}\sigma into a purely repulsive reference part u_0 and a smooth attractive perturbation w:
Weeks-Chandler-Andersen: repulsive forces set the structure of a dense liquid

Einstein's 1905 analysis of Brownian motion showed that a particle performing a random walk wanders off, on average, not in proportion to time but to its square root: the mean-squared displacement grows linearly,
Einstein's diffusion law: mean-squared displacement grows linearly in time

Green (1954) and Kubo (1957) showed that transport coefficients are time integrals of equilibrium correlation functions. For self-diffusion the relevant function is the velocity autocorrelation C(t)=\langle\vec v(0)\cdot\vec v(t)\rangle, and
Green-Kubo: the diffusion coefficient as the integral of the velocity autocorrelation
chemistrykit.VibrationalPartitionFunctio: Einstein (1907) treated each vibration as a quantum oscillator of frequency \nu, so its heat capacity depends on \Theta_{\text{vib}}/T with \Theta_{\text{vib}}=h\nu/k_B. VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic's heat capacity is this formula: it vanishes as T\to0 (the vibration is "frozen out") and approaches the classical equipartition value k_B per mode only once T is comparable to \Theta_{\text{vib}}. The second plot shows why a stiff mode (like Einstein's diamond) stays frozen out at temperatures where a soft mode already behaves classically.
Einstein's quantum theory of the vibrational heat capacity

James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"
Gibbs (1902) showed that for a system at fixed temperature every thermodynamic function follows from the canonical partition function Q=\sum_i e^{-E_i/k_BT}:
Gibbs's canonical ensemble: all thermodynamics from one partition function

James Clerk Maxwell (1860) and, in fully general form, Ludwig Boltzmann (1871) showed that every classical quadratic degree of freedom of a system in thermal equilibrium contributes exactly \frac12k_B to its heat capacity -- the equipartition theorem. A rigid diatomic molecule therefore "should" carry \frac32k_B (translation) + k_B (2 rotational degrees of freedom) + k_B (1 vibrational mode, kinetic + potential) = \frac72k_B at every temperature -- a prediction 19th-century equipartition theory could not explain deviations from (Maxwell himself flagged the puzzle sharply in 1879). Only VibrationalPartitionFunctionHarmonic is an exact quantum treatment in this package, so it alone shows the real resolution Einstein gave in 1907: a mode's contribution only "switches on" once k_BT exceeds its own quantum spacing. RotationalPartitionFunctionLinear, by contrast, implements only the classical high-temperature limit (as its own docstring flags), so it contributes its full k_B at every temperature here -- a deliberate approximation, harmless in practice because real rotational spacings are tiny compared to vibrational ones (as the numbers below confirm), but worth seeing explicitly rather than assuming.
The equipartition theorem, and why only one mode actually "freezes out"

chemistrykit.analytical.fit_calibration: The method of least squares picks the straight line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals S(m,b)=\sum_i(y_i-mx_i-b)^2. fit_calibration performs exactly that fit for a set of calibration standards; here we check that its slope sits at the bottom of the S(m) parabola, and that the residuals it leaves behind scatter around zero.
Legendre and Gauss's least squares: fitting a calibration line

Long and Winefordner argued that a detection limit should be tied to the calibration's own residual scatter s_{y/x} and slope m. lod and loq use the widely adopted calibration-based convention \text{LOD}=3.3\,s_{y/x}/m and \text{LOQ}=10\,s_{y/x}/m. A noisier method has proportionally higher limits.
Limits of detection and quantitation from a calibration curve
chemistrykit.analytical.gran_plot: gran_plot linearizes the buffer region of a weak-acid titration: V_b\,10^{-pH}=K_a(V_e-V_b). Plotting the left side against V_b gives a straight line whose x-intercept is the equivalence volume and whose slope is -K_a, so the endpoint follows from data taken well before it.
Gran plot: the equivalence point by linear extrapolation
chemistrykit.analytical.grubbs_critical_: grubbs_test computes G=\max_i|x_i-\bar x|/s and compares it with the critical value grubbs_critical_value, derived from Student's t distribution so that it exists for any sample size. A Monte Carlo run on outlier-free normal data confirms that the test falsely rejects a point at the nominal rate \alpha.
Grubbs' outlier test: the extreme value in standard deviations

chemistrykit.analytical.horrat: horwitz_rsd gives Horwitz's empirical expected between-laboratory RSD, 2^{1-0.5\log_{10}C}, which doubles for every 100-fold drop in concentration. chemistrykit.analytical.kovats_retention: Under isothermal gas chromatography, \log t' of the n-alkanes rises linearly with carbon number. Kováts placed every other compound on that ladder: kovats_retention_index interpolates \log t' between the bracketing alkanes, giving an index (n-octane = 800, n-nonane = 900, ...) that is far more transferable between instruments than a raw retention time.
Kováts retention indices from an n-alkane ladder
chemistrykit.analytical.minimum_plate_he: van_deemter_H evaluates H=A+B/u+Cu, the sum of eddy diffusion (`A`), longitudinal diffusion (`B/u`, dominant at low flow) and mass-transfer resistance (`Cu`, dominant at high flow). The competition between the last two gives a minimum plate height H_{min}=A+2\sqrt{BC} at u_{opt}=\sqrt{B/C} (~chemistrykit.analytical.minimum_plate_height, optimum_flow_velocity).
The van Deemter equation and the optimum flow velocity

An open capillary has no packing, so Golay's equation for it is the van Deemter equation with no eddy-diffusion term: H=B/u+Cu. Using van_deemter_H with A=0 for a capillary and A>0 for a packed column shows the lower plate height, and hence the many more plates a long capillary delivers.
Golay's open-tubular column: the van Deemter equation with A = 0

chemistrykit.analytical.plate_height: Treating a column as N equilibration stages ("theoretical plates") predicts a Gaussian peak whose width grows as t_R/\sqrt N. theoretical_plates inverts that: N=16(t_R/w_{base})^2=5.545(t_R/w_{1/2})^2, and plate_height gives the plate height H=L/N. Here we measure the widths of simulated peaks and recover the plate count they were built from.
Martin and Synge's theoretical plates from a peak's width
chemistrykit.analytical.purnell_resoluti: purnell_resolution writes resolution as R_s=\frac{\sqrt N}{4}\,\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}\,\frac{k_2}{1+k_2}. We check it against the direct peak-width formula resolution on simulated chromatograms, then compare the three levers: doubling N only multiplies R_s by \sqrt2, whereas a small change in selectivity \alpha can do much more.
Purnell's resolution equation: efficiency, selectivity, retention

chemistrykit.analytical.retention_factor: In Tsvet's experiment a pigment extract moves down a chalk column, each pigment at its own speed u/(1+k) set by how strongly it is retained (retention factor k). chemistrykit.analytical.savitzky_golay: savitzky_golay fits a low-order polynomial by least squares to each moving window and keeps its value (or derivative) at the center, which reduces to a fixed convolution with weights from savitzky_golay_coefficients -- e.g. (-3,12,17,12,-3)/35 for 5 points and a quadratic. Unlike a plain moving average, it removes noise with little flattening of narrow peaks, and it also gives smooth derivatives.

RedoxTitration computes the electrode potential during a redox titration from the Nernst equation, E=E^\circ-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q: before equivalence the analyte couple sets E, after it the titrant couple does. At half-equivalence E=E^\circ_1 exactly, at twice the equivalence volume E=E^\circ_2, and the endpoint is read, as in the laboratory, at the steepest rise of E.
The Nernst equation in a potentiometric redox titration

Here we measure the widths of simulated peaks and recover the plate count they were built from.
Martin and Synge's theoretical plates from a peak's width
chemistrykit.analytical.van_deemter_H: van_deemter_H evaluates H=A+B/u+Cu, the sum of eddy diffusion (`A`), longitudinal diffusion (`B/u`, dominant at low flow) and mass-transfer resistance (`Cu`, dominant at high flow). The competition between the last two gives a minimum plate height H_{min}=A+2\sqrt{BC} at u_{opt}=\sqrt{B/C} (~chemistrykit.analytical.minimum_plate_height, optimum_flow_velocity).
The van Deemter equation and the optimum flow velocity

An open capillary has no packing, so Golay's equation for it is the van Deemter equation with no eddy-diffusion term: H=B/u+Cu. Using van_deemter_H with A=0 for a capillary and A>0 for a packed column shows the lower plate height, and hence the many more plates a long capillary delivers.
Golay's open-tubular column: the van Deemter equation with A = 0

chemistrykit.constants.ATOMIC_MASS_UNIT: Trautz (1916) and Lewis (1918) computed a gas-phase rate constant as the number of collisions per unit time times the Boltzmann fraction with enough energy,
Trautz-Lewis collision theory: rate constants from molecular collisions

Born and Oppenheimer separated the fast electrons from the slow nuclei: first solve the electronic problem with the nuclei clamped at a fixed separation R, then let the nuclei move on the resulting potential energy curve U(R)=E_{el}(R)+e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0R. Here each point of the curve is a separate clamped-nuclei calculation with H2PlusVariational (``bond_length`` is a fixed input, never a dynamical variable). The curvature at the minimum then gives a nuclear vibrational frequency, and because the electronic curve does not depend on nuclear mass, H2+ and D2+ share the same curve but have different zero-point energies.
Born-Oppenheimer clamped-nuclei potential curve of H2+
chemistrykit.constants.ELECTRONVOLT: Hund and Mulliken's molecular-orbital theory builds one-electron orbitals spread over the whole molecule as a linear combination of atomic orbitals, \psi_\pm=c_A\chi_A\pm c_B\chi_B. H2PlusVariational does this for H2+ with one Gaussian orbital per proton: diagonalizing the 2x2 problem gives the in-phase bonding orbital (equal coefficients, energy below the isolated-atom level) and the out-of-phase antibonding orbital (opposite coefficients, energy above it). Following both orbital energies from short bond lengths out to separated atoms gives Mulliken's correlation diagram for the simplest molecule.
Hund-Mulliken LCAO molecular orbitals of H2+: bonding and antibonding

Born and Oppenheimer separated the fast electrons from the slow nuclei: first solve the electronic problem with the nuclei clamped at a fixed separation R, then let the nuclei move on the resulting potential energy curve U(R)=E_{el}(R)+e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0R. Here each point of the curve is a separate clamped-nuclei calculation with H2PlusVariational (``bond_length`` is a fixed input, never a dynamical variable). The curvature at the minimum then gives a nuclear vibrational frequency, and because the electronic curve does not depend on nuclear mass, H2+ and D2+ share the same curve but have different zero-point energies.
Born-Oppenheimer clamped-nuclei potential curve of H2+

G. N. Lewis's 1916 covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. In molecular-orbital language that pair is two electrons of opposite spin in the same bonding orbital. Using the two orbitals of a hydrogen-like diatomic from H2PlusVariational (at the H2 bond length, electron-electron repulsion neglected), fill them with 1 to 4 electrons: the bond order (n_{bonding}-n_{antibonding})/2 is 1 exactly when a single Lewis pair sits in the bonding orbital, and adding a second pair to the antibonding orbital cancels the bond (the He2 case).
Lewis's shared electron pair: two opposite-spin electrons in one bonding orbital

Helium was the first test of quantum mechanics beyond one electron. Kellner (1927) and Hylleraas (1928-1929) attacked it with the variational method: take both electrons in hydrogen-like 1s orbitals but let the nuclear charge they "see" be an adjustable \zeta. The energy E(\zeta)=(\zeta^2-2Z\zeta+\tfrac{5}{8}\zeta)E_h (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.helium.helium_like_variational_energy) is lowest at \zeta=Z-5/16=27/16 for helium (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.helium.optimize_helium_like_effective_charge): each electron shields the other from 5/16 of a nuclear charge. The result, -2.848\,E_h, is within 2% of the exact -2.9037\,E_h, which Hylleraas approached by adding the interelectronic distance to the trial function.
Kellner and Hylleraas: the variational helium atom and its screened charge

Schrodinger's first 1926 paper solved his wave equation for the hydrogen atom and recovered the Bohr energies E_n\propto-1/n^2 without any quantization postulate. HydrogenLikeAtom reproduces the textbook 13.6 eV hydrogen ground-state energy exactly, and its radial wavefunctions (built from the associated Laguerre polynomials of scipy.special) are independently checked here by numerically integrating them to a normalized probability of 1.
Schrodinger's hydrogen atom: radial wavefunctions and orbital energies

Hans Kuhn (1949) treated the pi electrons of a linear conjugated dye as free electrons in a one-dimensional box as long as the conjugated chain. With N pi electrons filling the box levels two at a time, the lowest absorption is the HOMO to LUMO jump, \Delta E=\frac{h^2}{8mL^2}(N+1), so a longer chain (more electrons and a longer box) absorbs at longer wavelength. conjugated_dye_absorption_wavelength implements this on top of ParticleInBox1D.
Kuhn's free-electron model of conjugated dye color
chemistrykit.constants.ELEMENTARY_CHARGE: Frenkel (1926) argued that at any T>0 some ions leave their sites for interstitial gaps, because the configurational entropy gained outweighs the enthalpy cost at low concentration. The equilibrium number is n_F=\sqrt{NN_i}\exp(-\Delta H_F/2k_BT) (~chemistrykit.crystal.systems.defects.frenkel_defect_concentration). AgCl, where small Ag+ ions readily occupy interstitial sites, is the textbook Frenkel-dominated solid (\Delta H_F\approx1.4 eV).
Frenkel defects: vacancy-interstitial pairs in silver chloride

Wagner and Schottky (1930) identified the second point-defect mechanism of ionic crystals: a cation and an anion leave the bulk together, keeping the crystal neutral and leaving a vacancy pair behind. The equilibrium number is n_S=N\exp(-\Delta H_S/2k_BT) (~chemistrykit.crystal.systems.defects.schottky_defect_concentration). In NaCl, the classic Schottky-dominated solid, \Delta H_S\approx2.3 eV.
Schottky defects: paired cation and anion vacancies in rock salt

Born and Lande (1918) balanced the Madelung attraction -A/r against a short-range repulsion B/r^n; setting dU/dr=0 at the observed spacing r_0 gives U=-\frac{N_AM|z_+z_-|e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0}(1-\frac{1}{n}), which BornLandeLatticeEnergy evaluates. This example shows the energy curve for NaCl and compares the equation with Born-Haber values for six rock-salt halides.
Born-Lande equation: lattice energies of the alkali halides

Madelung (1918) asked for the electrostatic energy of one ion in the field of every other ion of an infinite crystal. For rock salt it is U=-Me^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0) per ion pair, with the Madelung constant M=\sum_j \pm r_0/r_j summed shell by shell: 6 opposite charges at r_0, 12 like charges at \sqrt2r_0, 8 opposite charges at \sqrt3r_0, and so on. madelung_constant_nacl returns the converged value.
Madelung's lattice sum: the electrostatic energy of rock salt

Roothaan and Hall turned the molecular orbital problem into matrix algebra: expand each orbital in a finite, non-orthogonal basis and the variational condition becomes the generalized eigenvalue problem HC=SCE, solved here by solve_secular_equation. For the one-electron H2+ the Fock matrix is just the core Hamiltonian, so the equation is solved exactly once in each basis. The example shows that the overlap matrix S matters, that Lowdin's symmetric orthogonalization S^{-1/2}HS^{-1/2} gives the same answer, and that enlarging the basis lowers the energy toward the exact H2+ value, as the variational principle requires.
Roothaan-Hall equations: solving HC = SCE in a finite basis
chemistrykit.constants.FARADAY: The Butler-Volmer equation writes the net electrode current as the difference of an anodic and a cathodic exponential. At zero overpotential the two partial currents are equal (each is i_0) and cancel -- a dynamic equilibrium; far from equilibrium one term dominates and the equation becomes Tafel's straight line. This example plots both partial currents and butler_volmer_current_density, shows the effect of the transfer coefficient \alpha, and checks numerically how fast the Tafel limit is reached.
The Butler-Volmer equation: anodic and cathodic partial currents

Faraday's first law: the mass liberated at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, m = QM/(nF). His second law: for a fixed charge, different substances are liberated in proportion to their equivalent weights M/n. This example verifies both with faradays_law_mass and mass_from_charge, recovering the single universal constant -- the Faraday -- that links charge to chemical change.

Cottrell (1903) solved the diffusion problem for a planar electrode whose potential is suddenly stepped so that the electroactive species is consumed at the surface: the current decays as t^{-1/2}, i = nFAC\sqrt{D/(\pi t)}. This example plots cottrell_current, checks the constant i\sqrt{t} signature, and recovers the diffusion coefficient from a noisy "measured" transient via the Cottrell plot of i against t^{-1/2}.
The Cottrell equation: current decay after a potential step

Randles and Ševčík (1948) independently showed that the peak current of a reversible linear-sweep voltammogram grows with the square root of the scan rate, i_p = 0.4463\,nFAC\sqrt{nFvD/RT}. This example evaluates randles_sevcik_peak_current over a range of scan rates, and recovers the diffusion coefficient from the slope of the i_p vs. \sqrt{v} plot -- the standard diagnostic for a diffusion-controlled electrode reaction.
The Randles-Ševčík equation: peak current in cyclic voltammetry

Schrodinger's third 1926 paper introduced his perturbation theory; here it is applied to a harmonic oscillator with an added quartic term. Checks quartic_perturbation_first_order_correction's first-order Rayleigh-Schrodinger estimate against exact numerical diagonalization of the full anharmonic Hamiltonian (~chemistrykit.quantum.systems.perturbation.anharmonic_energy_levels, built in a truncated harmonic-oscillator basis via position_operator_matrix), and confirms that a cubic perturbation gives exactly zero first-order correction by parity.

Perrin (1926) related the polarization of fluorescence to how far a molecule rotates during its excited-state lifetime \tau: r=r_0/(1+\tau/\theta), with rotational correlation time \theta=\eta V/k_BT (~chemistrykit.photochem.perrin_anisotropy, rotational_correlation_time). A small dye depolarizes almost completely in water but stays polarized in viscous glycerol, and a "Perrin plot" of 1/r against T/\eta is a straight line whose intercept gives r_0 and whose slope gives the molecular volume.
Perrin equation: fluorescence anisotropy and molecular rotation

Ernst Ising (1925) solved the chain of spins s_i=\pm1 with nearest-neighbor coupling J and found no spontaneous magnetization at any temperature above zero. Ising1D solves it with the 2x2 transfer matrix, whose eigenvalues \lambda_\pm give Z_N=\lambda_+^N+\lambda_-^N exactly. The plots show a checked partition function, a magnetization that is a smooth function of field at every temperature (it only becomes a step at T=0), a correlation length that grows as e^{2J/k_BT} but stays finite, and a smooth heat-capacity maximum instead of a singularity.
Ising's one-dimensional chain: no phase transition
Kramers and Wannier (1941) showed that the square-lattice Ising model's high-temperature series at coupling K=J/k_BT equals its low-temperature series at the dual coupling K^*, with
Kramers-Wannier duality and the exact Ising critical temperature

Onsager (1944) computed the free energy of the square-lattice Ising model exactly: the first exact solution of a model with a genuine phase transition. Ising2DOnsager evaluates his free energy, internal energy, and heat capacity, together with Yang's (1952) spontaneous magnetization m=[1-\sinh^{-4}(2J/k_BT)]^{1/8}. The heat capacity diverges logarithmically at T_c, and the magnetization vanishes with exponent \beta=1/8. Neither the mean-field (Bragg-Williams) theory, shown for comparison, nor Ising's own one-dimensional chain reproduces these features.
Onsager's exact solution of the two-dimensional Ising model

Boltzmann's 1877 insight, written by Planck as S=k_B\ln W: entropy counts the microscopic arrangements W compatible with a macroscopic state. For N indistinguishable molecules on M lattice sites, W=\binom{M}{N}, and canonical_entropy evaluates k_B\ln W exactly via ln_binomial. The entropy is largest at half filling, where the number of arrangements peaks, and per site it converges to the Stirling-approximation mixing entropy -k_B[\theta\ln\theta+(1-\theta)\ln(1-\theta)] as M grows.
Boltzmann's S = k ln W by counting lattice arrangements
Gibbs (1902) showed that for a system at fixed temperature every thermodynamic function follows from the canonical partition function Q=\sum_i e^{-E_i/k_BT}:
Gibbs's canonical ensemble: all thermodynamics from one partition function
De Broglie's relation \lambda=h/p, averaged over a gas's thermal spread of momenta, gives the thermal de Broglie wavelength
De Broglie's matter waves: the thermal wavelength of a gas
Bose and Einstein (1924-25) and Fermi and Dirac (1926) found the mean occupancy of a single-particle state of energy \varepsilon for indistinguishable bosons and fermions:

Rahman's 1964 simulation followed 864 argon atoms interacting through a Lennard-Jones potential with \epsilon/k_B = 120\ \text{K} and \sigma = 3.4\ \text{\AA}, at T = 94.4\ \text{K} and a mass density of 1.374\ \text{g/cm}^3 -- liquid argon just above its triple point. Here the same state point is simulated with LJFluid (512 atoms, reduced units), and the radial distribution function (~chemistrykit.md.systems.lj_fluid.LJFluid.radial_distribution_function) is converted back to ångströms, as Rahman compared it with neutron- and X-ray-scattering data on real liquid argon.

Gibbs showed that the amount of a dilute solute held at a liquid surface, the surface excess \Gamma, follows from how the surface tension changes with concentration: \Gamma = -(1/RT)\,d\gamma/d\ln c. So a surfactant that lowers \gamma must be concentrated at the surface, and no one has to look at the surface itself. This example takes Szyszkowski-type surface-tension data (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.gibbs_adsorption.szyszkowski_surface_tension) for an aqueous fatty-acid-like solute and applies gibbs_surface_excess. It recovers a saturating Langmuir curve for \Gamma and, from the plateau, the area each adsorbed molecule occupies.
The Gibbs adsorption equation: surface excess from surface tension
chemistrykit.constants.PROTON_MASS: Born and Oppenheimer separated the fast electrons from the slow nuclei: first solve the electronic problem with the nuclei clamped at a fixed separation R, then let the nuclei move on the resulting potential energy curve U(R)=E_{el}(R)+e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0R. Here each point of the curve is a separate clamped-nuclei calculation with H2PlusVariational (``bond_length`` is a fixed input, never a dynamical variable). The curvature at the minimum then gives a nuclear vibrational frequency, and because the electronic curve does not depend on nuclear mass, H2+ and D2+ share the same curve but have different zero-point energies.
Born-Oppenheimer clamped-nuclei potential curve of H2+
chemistrykit.constants.R: The Butler-Volmer equation writes the net electrode current as the difference of an anodic and a cathodic exponential. At zero overpotential the two partial currents are equal (each is i_0) and cancel -- a dynamic equilibrium; far from equilibrium one term dominates and the equation becomes Tafel's straight line. This example plots both partial currents and butler_volmer_current_density, shows the effect of the transfer coefficient \alpha, and checks numerically how fast the Tafel limit is reached.
The Butler-Volmer equation: anodic and cathodic partial currents

Randles and Ševčík (1948) independently showed that the peak current of a reversible linear-sweep voltammogram grows with the square root of the scan rate, i_p = 0.4463\,nFAC\sqrt{nFvD/RT}. This example evaluates randles_sevcik_peak_current over a range of scan rates, and recovers the diffusion coefficient from the slope of the i_p vs. \sqrt{v} plot -- the standard diagnostic for a diffusion-controlled electrode reaction.
The Randles-Ševčík equation: peak current in cyclic voltammetry

Trautz-Lewis collision theory: rate constants from molecular collisions

Constable (1925) found that across a series of similar catalysts, a higher activation energy E_a came with a higher pre-exponential factor A, so \ln A rose linearly with E_a:

Polanyi (1914) described adsorption by the potential A = RT\ln(P_0/P) (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.polanyi_potential) and claimed that the filled pore volume depends on A alone, through one characteristic curve that does not change with temperature. Dubinin and Radushkevich (1947) gave that curve for microporous carbons as W = W_0\exp[-(A/E)^2] (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.dubinin_radushkevich_loading). Below, isotherms measured at three temperatures look different against P/P_0 but fall onto a single curve when replotted against A. A Dubinin-Radushkevich fit then recovers the pore volume W_0 and the characteristic energy E (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.fit_dubinin_radushkevich).
Polanyi's potential theory and the Dubinin-Radushkevich characteristic curve

For N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 the reaction quotient Q = x_{NO_2}^2/x_{N_2O_4} (at P = P^\circ), computed by reaction_quotient, rises monotonically with the extent of reaction. The law of mass action says the mixture stops changing where Q reaches the equilibrium constant K. Starting from different mixtures of reactant and product, the equilibrium compositions found by solve_equilibrium_composition all give the same Q = K.
Guldberg and Waage's law of mass action: Q = K at equilibrium

van't Hoff's equation d\ln K/dT = \Delta H^\circ/(RT^2) makes \ln K a straight line in 1/T with slope -\Delta H^\circ/R and intercept \Delta S^\circ/R. This example generates noisy equilibrium constants for N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 from van_t_hoff_equilibrium_constant and recovers the reaction enthalpy and entropy with fit_van_t_hoff.
The van't Hoff plot: ln K against 1/T
Two disturbances of N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2, an endothermic reaction that increases the number of gas molecules:
Le Chatelier's principle: equilibrium shifts that oppose a disturbance

For a reaction between perfect crystals, Nernst found that \Delta G and \Delta H approach each other with zero slope as T \to 0, so \Delta S = -\partial\Delta G/\partial T \to 0. With Debye T^3 heat capacities, \Delta C_p = \alpha T^3, the curves are \Delta H = \Delta H_0 + \alpha T^4/4, \Delta S = \alpha T^3/3, and \Delta G = \Delta H_0 - \alpha T^4/12. Planck's stronger form, S \to 0 for every perfect crystal, gives absolute entropies from calorimetry, S(T) = \int_0^T C_p/T'\,dT'. Those absolute entropies underlie the standard Gibbs energies of formation that gibbs_energy_of_mixture takes as input.
Nernst's heat theorem: reaction entropy vanishes at absolute zero

chemistrykit.constants.VACUUM_PERMITTIVI: Born and Lande (1918) balanced the Madelung attraction -A/r against a short-range repulsion B/r^n; setting dU/dr=0 at the observed spacing r_0 gives U=-\frac{N_AM|z_+z_-|e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0}(1-\frac{1}{n}), which BornLandeLatticeEnergy evaluates. Madelung (1918) asked for the electrostatic energy of one ion in the field of every other ion of an infinite crystal. For rock salt it is U=-Me^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0) per ion pair, with the Madelung constant M=\sum_j \pm r_0/r_j summed shell by shell: 6 opposite charges at r_0, 12 like charges at \sqrt2r_0, 8 opposite charges at \sqrt3r_0, and so on. madelung_constant_nacl returns the converged value.
Madelung's lattice sum: the electrostatic energy of rock salt

Roothaan and Hall turned the molecular orbital problem into matrix algebra: expand each orbital in a finite, non-orthogonal basis and the variational condition becomes the generalized eigenvalue problem HC=SCE, solved here by solve_secular_equation. For the one-electron H2+ the Fock matrix is just the core Hamiltonian, so the equation is solved exactly once in each basis. The example shows that the overlap matrix S matters, that Lowdin's symmetric orthogonalization S^{-1/2}HS^{-1/2} gives the same answer, and that enlarging the basis lowers the energy toward the exact H2+ value, as the variational principle requires.
Roothaan-Hall equations: solving HC = SCE in a finite basis

Christian Samuel Weiss (1815) sorted crystals into systems by the lengths of, and angles between, their crystallographic axes -- the idea that survives as today's 7 crystal systems. classify_crystal_system classifies a unit cell purely from the equalities/inequalities among its six lattice parameters (a,b,c,\alpha,\beta,\gamma), and unit_cell_volume gives the general-cell volume formula that reduces to familiar shortcuts (abc, \frac{\sqrt3}{2}a^2c) in special cases.

Nicolas Steno (1669) found that quartz crystals, however unevenly grown, always meet at the same angles between corresponding faces. The angle between two faces depends only on their Miller indices -- not on how big the faces are -- which interplanar_angle_cubic computes for a cubic crystal from the face normals.

Hauy (1784-1801) argued that every natural crystal face cuts the three axes at intercepts in small whole-number ratios. miller_indices_from_intercepts turns those rational intercepts into the integer Miller indices (hkl) by taking reciprocals and clearing fractions; the (hkl) triple then fixes each face's interplanar spacing.

chemistrykit.crystal.systems.defects.fre: Frenkel (1926) argued that at any T>0 some ions leave their sites for interstitial gaps, because the configurational entropy gained outweighs the enthalpy cost at low concentration. The equilibrium number is n_F=\sqrt{NN_i}\exp(-\Delta H_F/2k_BT) (~chemistrykit.crystal.systems.defects.frenkel_defect_concentration). AgCl, where small Ag+ ions readily occupy interstitial sites, is the textbook Frenkel-dominated solid (\Delta H_F\approx1.4 eV).
Frenkel defects: vacancy-interstitial pairs in silver chloride
chemistrykit.crystal.systems.defects.sch: Wagner and Schottky (1930) identified the second point-defect mechanism of ionic crystals: a cation and an anion leave the bulk together, keeping the crystal neutral and leaving a vacancy pair behind. The equilibrium number is n_S=N\exp(-\Delta H_S/2k_BT) (~chemistrykit.crystal.systems.defects.schottky_defect_concentration). In NaCl, the classic Schottky-dominated solid, \Delta H_S\approx2.3 eV.
Schottky defects: paired cation and anion vacancies in rock salt
chemistrykit.crystal.systems.lattice_ene: Born and Lande (1918) balanced the Madelung attraction -A/r against a short-range repulsion B/r^n; setting dU/dr=0 at the observed spacing r_0 gives U=-\frac{N_AM|z_+z_-|e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0}(1-\frac{1}{n}), which BornLandeLatticeEnergy evaluates. This example shows the energy curve for NaCl and compares the equation with Born-Haber values for six rock-salt halides.
Born-Lande equation: lattice energies of the alkali halides

Kapustinskii (1956) replaced the structure-specific Madelung constant with a near-universal constant per ion, so KapustinskiiLatticeEnergy needs only the number of ions per formula unit, the charges, and the ionic radii. On rock-salt halides it tracks the structure-based Born-Lande value; it also handles salts of other structures (fluorite CaF2) where no Madelung constant is supplied at all.
Kapustinskii equation: lattice energy without a crystal structure

Madelung (1918) asked for the electrostatic energy of one ion in the field of every other ion of an infinite crystal. For rock salt it is U=-Me^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0r_0) per ion pair, with the Madelung constant M=\sum_j \pm r_0/r_j summed shell by shell: 6 opposite charges at r_0, 12 like charges at \sqrt2r_0, 8 opposite charges at \sqrt3r_0, and so on. madelung_constant_nacl returns the converged value.
Madelung's lattice sum: the electrostatic energy of rock salt
chemistrykit.crystal.systems.packing.Bod: Kepler (1611) guessed that no stacking of equal spheres fills space more densely than the layered (face-centered cubic / hexagonal close) packing, with fraction \pi/\sqrt{18}\approx0.7405. Comparing the four textbook lattices shows the close-packed pair at exactly that bound.
Kepler's conjecture: packing efficiency of SC, BCC, FCC, and HCP

chemistrykit.crystal.systems.xrd.XRDPeak: Each line of a diffraction pattern is a family of (hkl) planes that satisfies Bragg's law n\lambda=2d\sin\theta. powder_xrd_peaks computes each reflection's structure factor (~chemistrykit.crystal.systems.xrd.structure_factor) directly from atomic positions and Miller indices, so BCC's and FCC's systematic absences (reflections with zero intensity by symmetry) fall out automatically rather than being hardcoded as a rule.
Bragg's law: indexing powder XRD peaks

Scherrer (1918) showed that tiny crystallites give broadened powder lines, with width \beta=K\lambda/(\tau\cos\theta) for crystallite size \tau. scherrer_crystallite_size inverts this: here, copper powder patterns are broadened for three crystallite sizes, and each size is recovered from the measured width of the (111) line.
Scherrer equation: crystallite size from peak broadening
chemistrykit.crystal.systems.xrd.d_spaci: Hauy (1784-1801) argued that every natural crystal face cuts the three axes at intercepts in small whole-number ratios. miller_indices_from_intercepts turns those rational intercepts into the integer Miller indices (hkl) by taking reciprocals and clearing fractions; the (hkl) triple then fixes each face's interplanar spacing.
Hauy's law of rational indices: Miller indices from face intercepts

Von Laue (1912) predicted that a crystal, as a periodic array of scatterers, should diffract X-rays like a grating, and Friedrich and Knipping saw the discrete spots. Summing the waves from N periodically spaced scatterers with structure_factor gives the Laue interference function: intensity N^2 at integer h (the Laue condition) and almost nothing in between, ever sharper as N grows.
Laue's interference: sharp diffraction spots from a periodic array

Shannon (1976) fitted one self-consistent radius per ion (for a given coordination number) so that cation-anion distances in thousands of crystals are reproduced by simple sums r_++r_-. chemistrykit.electrochem.BatteryDischarg: Peukert's 1897 power law, t = C_p/I^k, says a lead-acid battery discharged faster delivers less total charge. Using effective_capacity, this example compares the ideal Peukert exponent k=1 (same capacity at every rate) with a realistic k=1.2, then draws discharge curves from ConstantCurrentBattery (a deliberately simplified model; see its docstring) whose runtimes shrink faster than 1/I.

chemistrykit.electrochem.HalfReaction: Days after learning of Volta's newly announced pile, William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle connected one to a bowl of water in May 1800 and watched gas bubble from each wire -- the first electrolysis, and the first new discovery the pile made possible. This example reconstructs both halves of that observation from functions already in this package: the theoretical minimum decomposition voltage of water (~chemistrykit.electrochem.systems.electrolysis.minimum_applied_voltage_electrolytic, applied to the tabulated H+/H2 and O2/H2O standard potentials) comes out at the textbook 1.23 V, and Faraday's law (~chemistrykit.electrochem.systems.electrolysis.moles_from_charge) recovers the 2:1 hydrogen-to-oxygen ratio Nicholson and Carlisle actually saw bubbling from the two wires, directly from electron-transfer stoichiometry.
Nicholson and Carlisle's electrolysis of water
chemistrykit.electrochem.KohlrauschFit: Kohlrausch found that the molar conductivity of a strong electrolyte falls linearly with \sqrt{c}, \Lambda_m = \Lambda_m^\circ - K\sqrt{c}, and that the infinite-dilution value \Lambda_m^\circ is a sum of independent ionic contributions. This example extrapolates noisy KCl data to infinite dilution with fit_kohlrausch_law, and uses limiting_molar_conductivity for his classic trick: the limiting conductivity of the weak acid acetic acid, which cannot be extrapolated, from three strong electrolytes.
Kohlrausch's laws: independent migration and the square-root law
chemistrykit.electrochem.TafelFit: Tafel (1905) found that far from equilibrium the overpotential of hydrogen evolution grows linearly with \log_{10} i: \eta = b\log_{10}(i/i_0). This example generates noisy "measured" high-overpotential data, draws the Tafel plot, and uses fit_tafel_plot to recover the Tafel slope b and exchange current density i_0 by linear regression -- the analysis Tafel's successors still use, and compares the slope with tafel_slope's textbook ~118 mV/decade for \alpha = 0.5, n = 1.
Tafel's law: overpotential linear in log current

The Butler-Volmer equation writes the net electrode current as the difference of an anodic and a cathodic exponential. At zero overpotential the two partial currents are equal (each is i_0) and cancel -- a dynamic equilibrium; far from equilibrium one term dominates and the equation becomes Tafel's straight line. This example plots both partial currents and butler_volmer_current_density, shows the effect of the transfer coefficient \alpha, and checks numerically how fast the Tafel limit is reached.
The Butler-Volmer equation: anodic and cathodic partial currents

Faraday's first law: the mass liberated at an electrode is proportional to the charge passed, m = QM/(nF). His second law: for a fixed charge, different substances are liberated in proportion to their equivalent weights M/n. This example verifies both with faradays_law_mass and mass_from_charge, recovering the single universal constant -- the Faraday -- that links charge to chemical change.

In 1807 Humphry Davy passed current through molten potash and soda and isolated potassium and sodium -- metals no chemical reducing agent of the day could free, because their reduction potentials are among the most negative in the electrochemical series. This example ranks Davy's two couples against the rest of STANDARD_REDUCTION_POTENTIALS, shows why the common reducing metals (Zn, Fe) cannot reduce K+ or Na+, computes the minimum electrolysis voltage for the molten chlorides with minimum_applied_voltage_electrolytic, and uses Faraday's law to estimate how much potassium a current yields.
Davy's electrolytic isolation of potassium and sodium

chemistrykit.electrochem.systems.voltamm: Cottrell (1903) solved the diffusion problem for a planar electrode whose potential is suddenly stepped so that the electroactive species is consumed at the surface: the current decays as t^{-1/2}, i = nFAC\sqrt{D/(\pi t)}. This example plots cottrell_current, checks the constant i\sqrt{t} signature, and recovers the diffusion coefficient from a noisy "measured" transient via the Cottrell plot of i against t^{-1/2}.
The Cottrell equation: current decay after a potential step

Heyrovský's dropping mercury electrode (1922) records a sigmoidal "polarographic wave" for each reducible species: its position (the half-wave potential) identifies the species and its height (the diffusion current, given by Ilkovič's 1934 equation) measures its concentration. This example builds a two-component polarogram from polarographic_wave_current with wave heights from ilkovic_diffusion_current, and shows the linear calibration of diffusion current against concentration.
Heyrovský's polarography and the Ilkovič equation

Randles and Ševčík (1948) independently showed that the peak current of a reversible linear-sweep voltammogram grows with the square root of the scan rate, i_p = 0.4463\,nFAC\sqrt{nFvD/RT}. This example evaluates randles_sevcik_peak_current over a range of scan rates, and recovers the diffusion coefficient from the slope of the i_p vs. \sqrt{v} plot -- the standard diagnostic for a diffusion-controlled electrode reaction.
The Randles-Ševčík equation: peak current in cyclic voltammetry

Using effective_capacity, this example compares the ideal Peukert exponent k=1 (same capacity at every rate) with a realistic k=1.2, then draws discharge curves from ConstantCurrentBattery (a deliberately simplified model; see its docstring) whose runtimes shrink faster than 1/I.

The Butler-Volmer equation writes the net electrode current as the difference of an anodic and a cathodic exponential. At zero overpotential the two partial currents are equal (each is i_0) and cancel -- a dynamic equilibrium; far from equilibrium one term dominates and the equation becomes Tafel's straight line. This example plots both partial currents and butler_volmer_current_density, shows the effect of the transfer coefficient \alpha, and checks numerically how fast the Tafel limit is reached.
The Butler-Volmer equation: anodic and cathodic partial currents

chemistrykit.kinetics.FirstOrder: van't Hoff (1884) classified reactions by the order n of their rate law -d[A]/dt = k[A]^n. The three textbook cases -- ZeroOrder, FirstOrder, and SecondOrder -- all started from the same initial concentration and with rate constants chosen to give the same half-life, so the different curvature (linear, exponential, hyperbolic) is the only thing distinguishing them. First order is the only one whose half-life doesn't depend on the starting concentration; the plot below marks all three half-lives to make that concrete.
van't Hoff's reaction orders: zero-, first-, and second-order rate laws

Wilhelmy (1850) followed the acid-catalyzed inversion of cane sugar by polarimetry: the optical rotation \alpha(t) drifts from the dextrorotatory sucrose value towards the (levorotatory) value of the glucose + fructose mixture. Because \alpha is linear in the concentrations, \alpha(t) - \alpha_\infty is proportional to the sucrose still present, and a straight line of \ln[(\alpha - \alpha_\infty)/(\alpha_0 - \alpha_\infty)] against t identifies -d[\text{sugar}]/dt = k[\text{sugar}].
Wilhelmy's sucrose inversion: the first measured first-order rate law

This example draws that saturation curve with its two limiting regimes, integrates the substrate-depletion progress curve an assay actually records, and shows how competitive and noncompetitive inhibitors distort the curve.
Michaelis and Menten's saturating enzyme rate law
Bodenstein (1913) set the net rate of change of a short-lived intermediate to zero; Lindemann (1922) used exactly that trick on the energized molecule A^* of the mechanism
Bodenstein's steady-state approximation and Lindemann's unimolecular fall-off

StoichiometricNetwork's general mass-action engine, applied to a three-step radical chain mechanism (initiation, branching propagation, and linear termination), reproduces the qualitative signature of a chain-branching explosion: below a critical branching rate the radical concentration stays small and the fuel decays gently, while above it the radical population grows explosively and burns through the fuel in a short, sharp spike -- exactly the ignition-vs-no-ignition switch behind Semenov's and Hinshelwood's explosion-limit theory.
Chain-branching explosions and Semenov's critical condition
Bateman (1910) solved the chain of first-order steps A \xrightarrow{k_1} B \xrightarrow{k_2} C (written for radioactive decay series, but identical for consecutive chemical reactions) in closed form:
Bateman's closed-form solution for consecutive reactions

Eigen (1954) measured reactions far too fast to mix by perturbing an equilibrium mixture (a sudden temperature, pressure, or field jump) and timing its exponential return to the new equilibrium. For A \rightleftharpoons B the relaxation time is \tau = 1/(k_f + k_r), so combining \tau with the equilibrium constant K = k_f/k_r yields both rate constants. For the association A + B \rightleftharpoons C linearizing about equilibrium gives 1/\tau = k_f([A]_{eq} + [B]_{eq}) + k_r, the formula Eigen used to show that H^+ + OH^- recombination is diffusion-controlled.
Eigen's chemical relaxation: temperature jump and relaxation time

For two competing channels A \xrightarrow{k_1} B and A \xrightarrow{k_2} C, the reactant decays with the sum k_1 + k_2, while the product ratio [B]/[C] = k_1/k_2 is fixed at every instant -- the kinetic basis of product selectivity. Integrated with parallel.

Lotka's autocatalytic oscillator and its neutral orbits

Field and Noyes (1974) boiled the FKN mechanism of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction -- cerium-catalyzed oxidation of malonic acid by bromate -- down to three intermediates: HBrO\ 2 (x), bromide (y), and the oxidized catalyst Ce(IV) (z). The resulting "Oregonator" (~chemistrykit.kinetics.systems.oscillators.Oregonator) produces the BZ reaction's hallmark relaxation oscillations: long quiet stretches while bromide is slowly consumed, then an autocatalytic burst of HBrO\ 2 that oxidizes the catalyst (the colour flash seen by Belousov), which in turn regenerates bromide and shuts the burst off. Raising the stoichiometric factor f well above 2 stabilizes the steady state and the oscillation disappears.
The Oregonator: oscillations of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction

Bodenstein (1913) measured that one absorbed photon forms up to 10^5-10^6 HCl molecules in an illuminated H2/Cl2 mixture, apparently violating photochemical equivalence. Nernst (1918) explained it: the photon only splits one Cl2 into two Cl atoms, which then start a chain (Cl + H2 -> HCl + H, H + Cl2 -> HCl + Cl) that runs until two atoms recombine. hydrogen_chlorine_chain_network integrates this mechanism, and chain_quantum_yield gives the steady-state yield \Phi=2k_2[\mathrm{H_2}]/\sqrt{k_t I_{abs}}. Rate constants are in arbitrary consistent units.
Bodenstein and Nernst: the H2 + Cl2 photochemical chain reaction

jablonski_network builds the 3-state (S1, T1, S0) Jablonski excited-state decay network as a StoichiometricNetwork -- reusing the kinetics domain's general mass-action reaction-network engine rather than reimplementing rate-equation integration. The numerical integration is checked here against jablonski_populations_analytic's closed-form solution.

A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. Because termination is much faster than initiator decomposition, the radical concentration relaxes almost immediately to the steady-state approximation's closed-form prediction (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.steady_state_radical_concentration) -- verified here by comparing the two directly -- while monomer is consumed only slowly, at the classic square-root-of-initiator rate.
Flory's steady-state kinetics of free-radical polymerization

free_radical_network's mode argument selects between the two ways two growing radical chains can terminate: combination (they fuse into a single dead chain) or disproportionation (one radical abstracts a hydrogen from the other, producing two separate dead chains). Bevington, Melville, and Taylor ("The Termination Reaction in Radical Polymerizations," J. Polym. Sci. 12 (1954), 449-459) showed how to distinguish the two experimentally, by end-group analysis and by the resulting degree of polymerization's relationship to the kinetic chain length (~chemistrykit.polymer.systems.chain_growth.kinetic_chain_length) nu: \bar X_n = 2\nu for combination (two radicals' worth of monomer per dead chain) but \bar X_n = \nu for disproportionation (one radical's worth per dead chain) -- verified here directly against the numerically integrated network.

Bodenstein (1913) measured that one absorbed photon forms up to 10^5-10^6 HCl molecules in an illuminated H2/Cl2 mixture, apparently violating photochemical equivalence. Nernst (1918) explained it: the photon only splits one Cl2 into two Cl atoms, which then start a chain (Cl + H2 -> HCl + H, H + Cl2 -> HCl + Cl) that runs until two atoms recombine. hydrogen_chlorine_chain_network integrates this mechanism, and chain_quantum_yield gives the steady-state yield \Phi=2k_2[\mathrm{H_2}]/\sqrt{k_t I_{abs}}. Rate constants are in arbitrary consistent units.

A photoswitch A <-> B under simultaneous forward and reverse photolysis reaches a photostationary state (PSS) rather than running to completion. photoswitch_network reuses reversible directly, and photostationary_state gives the exact algebraic PSS composition -- checked here against direct long-time numerical integration of the ODE system.
Photostationary-state kinetics of a two-state photoswitch

free_radical_network builds the lumped initiation/propagation/termination kinetics as a StoichiometricNetwork and integrates it numerically. chemistrykit.kinetics.MichaelisMentenFit: Lineweaver and Burk (1934) inverted the Michaelis-Menten equation into a straight line, 1/v = (K_m/V_{max})(1/[S]) + 1/V_{max}, so V_{max} and K_m could be read off the intercept and slope. fit_lineweaver_burk does exactly that fit on noisy initial-rate data. The second panel shows the method's well-known weakness: the same small relative noise becomes a large scatter at the low-[S] (large 1/[S]) end, which dominates the fitted line.
chemistrykit.kinetics.MichaelisMentenPro: Michaelis and Menten (1913) showed that an enzyme-catalyzed rate saturates with substrate, v = V_{max}[S]/(K_m + [S]), reaching exactly half of V_{max} at [S] = K_m. This example draws that saturation curve with its two limiting regimes, integrates the substrate-depletion progress curve an assay actually records, and shows how competitive and noncompetitive inhibitors distort the curve.
Michaelis and Menten's saturating enzyme rate law

chemistrykit.kinetics.Oregonator: Field and Noyes (1974) boiled the FKN mechanism of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky (BZ) reaction -- cerium-catalyzed oxidation of malonic acid by bromate -- down to three intermediates: HBrO\ 2 (x), bromide (y), and the oxidized catalyst Ce(IV) (z). The resulting "Oregonator" (~chemistrykit.kinetics.systems.oscillators.Oregonator) produces the BZ reaction's hallmark relaxation oscillations: long quiet stretches while bromide is slowly consumed, then an autocatalytic burst of HBrO\ 2 that oxidizes the catalyst (the colour flash seen by Belousov), which in turn regenerates bromide and shuts the burst off. Raising the stoichiometric factor f well above 2 stabilizes the steady state and the oscillation disappears.
The Oregonator: oscillations of the Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction

chemistrykit.kinetics.RateLaw: van't Hoff (1884) classified reactions by the order n of their rate law -d[A]/dt = k[A]^n. The three textbook cases -- ZeroOrder, FirstOrder, and SecondOrder -- all started from the same initial concentration and with rate constants chosen to give the same half-life, so the different curvature (linear, exponential, hyperbolic) is the only thing distinguishing them. First order is the only one whose half-life doesn't depend on the starting concentration; the plot below marks all three half-lives to make that concrete.
van't Hoff's reaction orders: zero-, first-, and second-order rate laws

Wilhelmy (1850) followed the acid-catalyzed inversion of cane sugar by polarimetry: the optical rotation \alpha(t) drifts from the dextrorotatory sucrose value towards the (levorotatory) value of the glucose + fructose mixture. Because \alpha is linear in the concentrations, \alpha(t) - \alpha_\infty is proportional to the sucrose still present, and a straight line of \ln[(\alpha - \alpha_\infty)/(\alpha_0 - \alpha_\infty)] against t identifies -d[\text{sugar}]/dt = k[\text{sugar}].
Wilhelmy's sucrose inversion: the first measured first-order rate law
