Arrhenius's k = Ae^{-E_a/RT} explains why a catalyst's lower activation energy multiplies the rate by e^{\Delta E_a/RT} (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.catalysis.compare_catalyzed_rate). Ostwald's definition adds the key condition that a catalyst cannot move the equilibrium. It lowers the barrier for the forward and the reverse reaction by the same amount, so both rate constants grow by the same factor and K = k_f/k_r does not change. Below, the reversible reaction A \rightleftharpoons B reaches equilibrium far sooner with the catalyst, and it reaches exactly the same equilibrium.

chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.Dub: Polanyi (1914) described adsorption by the potential A = RT\ln(P_0/P) (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.polanyi_potential) and claimed that the filled pore volume depends on A alone, through one characteristic curve that does not change with temperature. Dubinin and Radushkevich (1947) gave that curve for microporous carbons as W = W_0\exp[-(A/E)^2] (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.dubinin_radushkevich_loading). Below, isotherms measured at three temperatures look different against P/P_0 but fall onto a single curve when replotted against A. A Dubinin-Radushkevich fit then recovers the pore volume W_0 and the characteristic energy E (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.dubinin.fit_dubinin_radushkevich).
Polanyi's potential theory and the Dubinin-Radushkevich characteristic curve

chemistrykit.surface.systems.eley_rideal: In the Eley-Rideal mechanism (Eley and Rideal, 1940) only reactant A adsorbs. B reacts with adsorbed A straight from the gas phase, so the rate is k\theta_AP_B (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.eley_rideal.er_rate). A and B never compete for sites, so raising P_A can only help: the rate rises and levels off, and it stays first order in P_B. In the dual-site Langmuir-Hinshelwood mechanism (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.langmuir_hinshelwood.lh_rate_dual_site), too much A pushes B off the surface and the rate turns over. That difference is the standard kinetic test for telling the two mechanisms apart.
The Eley-Rideal mechanism: a gas molecule strikes an adsorbed one
FreundlichIsotherm models the empirical power law q=K_fP^{1/n}, useful for a heterogeneous surface where Langmuir's single-site-energy assumption breaks down. Unlike Langmuir, it has no saturation limit, so extrapolating it far beyond the fitted pressure range is unphysical. fit_freundlich recovers (Kf, n) via the standard log q vs. log P linearization.

chemistrykit.surface.systems.gibbs_adsor: Gibbs showed that the amount of a dilute solute held at a liquid surface, the surface excess \Gamma, follows from how the surface tension changes with concentration: \Gamma = -(1/RT)\,d\gamma/d\ln c. So a surfactant that lowers \gamma must be concentrated at the surface, and no one has to look at the surface itself. This example takes Szyszkowski-type surface-tension data (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.gibbs_adsorption.szyszkowski_surface_tension) for an aqueous fatty-acid-like solute and applies gibbs_surface_excess. It recovers a saturating Langmuir curve for \Gamma and, from the plateau, the area each adsorbed molecule occupies.
The Gibbs adsorption equation: surface excess from surface tension

chemistrykit.surface.systems.langmuir.La: LangmuirIsotherm models monolayer adsorption on a fixed pool of identical surface sites. Its fractional coverage \theta=KP/(1+KP) reaches exactly one-half at the half-saturation pressure P=1/K, and fit_langmuir recovers (K, qmax) from noisy loading-vs-pressure data via the standard 1/q-vs-1/P linearization.

Balandin's multiplet theory (1929) predicted that when catalytic activity is plotted against binding strength across a series of catalysts, it rises, peaks and falls again, tracing a "volcano". Bligaard, Norskov and coworkers (2004) later derived that shape from the Bronsted-Evans-Polanyi relation. This example reproduces the volcano with the standard textbook toy model (Chorkendorff & Niemantsverdriet, Concepts of Modern Catalysis and Kinetics, 2nd ed., Wiley-VCH, 2007, Ch. 8). The rate needs an occupied site to hold the intermediate and an empty site for the next step, so rate \propto\theta(1-\theta), with \theta the Langmuir coverage (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.langmuir.langmuir_coverage). The adsorption constant K stands in for binding strength. A hypothetical series of catalysts sits on the two legs of the volcano, and its summit is exactly Langmuir's half-saturation point K = 1/P. This is not a literal reproduction of Balandin's multiplet equations.
Balandin's volcano curve: catalytic activity peaks at intermediate binding

chemistrykit.surface.systems.tpd.TPDResu: In a TPD experiment a covered surface is heated at a steady rate \beta while the desorbing gas is recorded, and each binding state shows up as a peak. simulate_tpd integrates the Polanyi-Wigner rate equation to produce these spectra. Below, the formula is checked against the exact peak condition (~chemistrykit.surface.systems.tpd.first_order_peak_temperature). First-order peaks shift with heating rate but not with coverage, while second-order peaks move to lower temperature as the coverage rises.

chemistrykit.thermo.BinaryIdealSolution: Raoult's law, P_A = x_A P_A^* (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.raoult_vapor_pressure), makes each partial vapor pressure a straight line in liquid mole fraction. chemistrykit.thermo.ClausiusClapeyron: Water's liquid-vapor phase boundary from the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.phase_equilibria.ClausiusClapeyron), anchored at the normal boiling point. Plotting \ln P against 1/T gives a straight line of slope -\Delta H_{vap}/R; from_two_points recovers \Delta H_{vap} from two measured points, and boiling_point inverts the curve to find the boiling point at altitude.
The Clausius-Clapeyron vapor-pressure curve of water

Gibbs's phase rule, F = C - P + 2 (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.phase_equilibria.gibbs_phase_rule), says how many intensive variables can change while a set of phases coexists. On a one-component phase diagram, single-phase regions are areas (F=2), two-phase boundaries are curves (F=1), and three phases meet only at a point (F=0). The sketch below draws water's diagram around its triple point (vaporization and sublimation curves from the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, melting line from the Clapeyron slope) and labels each feature with its degrees of freedom.

chemistrykit.thermo.EquationOfState: Clapeyron's 1834 combined gas law unites Boyle's law (PV constant at fixed T), Charles's and Gay-Lussac's law (V \propto T at fixed P), and Avogadro's hypothesis into PV_m = RT. This example draws both classic views with IdealGas: hyperbolic Boyle isotherms, and straight Charles isobars that all extrapolate to zero volume at absolute zero.
Clapeyron's ideal gas law, PV = RT

Redlich and Kwong divided van der Waals's attraction term by \sqrt{T}. This example draws CO2 P-V isotherms well above and just below the critical temperature from RedlichKwong, with VanDerWaals and IdealGas for comparison. Both real-gas equations are built from CO2's critical temperature and pressure alone via from_critical_constants. Redlich-Kwong's universal critical compressibility factor is 1/3, closer to real gases than van der Waals's 3/8.
Redlich-Kwong isotherms of CO2 against van der Waals and the ideal gas

Peng and Robinson tuned the temperature dependence of their attraction term, \alpha(T), to Pitzer's acentric factor \omega so that the equation reproduces pure-fluid vapor pressures. This example computes the CO2 vapor-pressure curve predicted by PengRobinson (\omega = 0.224) with saturation_pressure, and compares it with van der Waals and Redlich-Kwong built from the same critical constants. Only Peng-Robinson passes through Pitzer's defining point, \log_{10}(P_{sat}/P_c) = -1 - \omega at T/T_c = 0.7.
Peng-Robinson: vapor pressures from the acentric factor

G. N. Lewis replaced pressure by the fugacity f = \phi P so that the ideal-gas form \mu = \mu^\circ + RT\ln(f/P^\circ) stays exact for real fluids. The left panel shows the fugacity coefficient \phi of supercritical CO2 computed by fugacity_coefficient from three equations of state. The right panel shows Lewis's phase-equilibrium criterion: below T_c the liquid and vapor fugacities from fugacity cross exactly at the saturation pressure.
Lewis fugacity: the effective pressure of a real gas

van't Hoff found that a dilute solution's osmotic pressure (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.osmotic_pressure) equals the pressure the solute particles would exert as an ideal gas at the same concentration and temperature. The factor i counts particles per formula unit: 1 for sucrose, about 2 for NaCl. The same factor multiplies the other colligative effects, freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.freezing_point_depression, boiling_point_elevation).
van't Hoff's osmotic pressure law, Pi = iMRT
chemistrykit.thermo.EquationOfState.from: Andrews's CO2 isotherms showed a flat liquid-vapor plateau below a critical temperature and none above it. chemistrykit.thermo.EquilibriumCompositi: For N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 the reaction quotient Q = x_{NO_2}^2/x_{N_2O_4} (at P = P^\circ), computed by reaction_quotient, rises monotonically with the extent of reaction. The law of mass action says the mixture stops changing where Q reaches the equilibrium constant K. Starting from different mixtures of reactant and product, the equilibrium compositions found by solve_equilibrium_composition all give the same Q = K.
Guldberg and Waage's law of mass action: Q = K at equilibrium

Gibbs showed that at fixed temperature and pressure a system reaches equilibrium at the minimum of its total Gibbs energy G = \sum_i n_i\mu_i. For N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 this example plots G(\xi) from gibbs_energy_of_mixture at several temperatures and marks the composition returned by solve_equilibrium_composition, which sits at each minimum. The slope dG/d\xi = \sum_i\nu_i\mu_i (the reaction Gibbs energy) crosses zero there.
Gibbs's equilibrium criterion: minimum total Gibbs energy

Le Chatelier's principle: equilibrium shifts that oppose a disturbance

chemistrykit.thermo.MargulesSolution: Margules wrote the activity coefficients of a binary liquid as power series in mole fraction. The one-parameter form used by MargulesSolution, \ln\gamma_1 = A x_2^2 and \ln\gamma_2 = A x_1^2, turns Raoult's straight lines into curves: A > 0 (unlike molecules repel) bows the total pressure upward and can produce a maximum-pressure azeotrope, while A < 0 bows it downward. The model still obeys the Gibbs-Duhem relation, and each component tends to Henry's law at infinite dilution.

chemistrykit.thermo.systems.EquilibriumC: For N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 the reaction quotient Q = x_{NO_2}^2/x_{N_2O_4} (at P = P^\circ), computed by reaction_quotient, rises monotonically with the extent of reaction. The law of mass action says the mixture stops changing where Q reaches the equilibrium constant K. Starting from different mixtures of reactant and product, the equilibrium compositions found by solve_equilibrium_composition all give the same Q = K.

Gibbs showed that at fixed temperature and pressure a system reaches equilibrium at the minimum of its total Gibbs energy G = \sum_i n_i\mu_i. For N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2 this example plots G(\xi) from gibbs_energy_of_mixture at several temperatures and marks the composition returned by solve_equilibrium_composition, which sits at each minimum. The slope dG/d\xi = \sum_i\nu_i\mu_i (the reaction Gibbs energy) crosses zero there.
Gibbs's equilibrium criterion: minimum total Gibbs energy

The slope dG/d\xi = \sum_i\nu_i\mu_i (the reaction Gibbs energy) crosses zero there.

For a reaction between perfect crystals, Nernst found that \Delta G and \Delta H approach each other with zero slope as T \to 0, so \Delta S = -\partial\Delta G/\partial T \to 0. With Debye T^3 heat capacities, \Delta C_p = \alpha T^3, the curves are \Delta H = \Delta H_0 + \alpha T^4/4, \Delta S = \alpha T^3/3, and \Delta G = \Delta H_0 - \alpha T^4/12. Planck's stronger form, S \to 0 for every perfect crystal, gives absolute entropies from calorimetry, S(T) = \int_0^T C_p/T'\,dT'. Those absolute entropies underlie the standard Gibbs energies of formation that gibbs_energy_of_mixture takes as input.
Nernst's heat theorem: reaction entropy vanishes at absolute zero

The one-parameter form used by MargulesSolution, \ln\gamma_1 = A x_2^2 and \ln\gamma_2 = A x_1^2, turns Raoult's straight lines into curves: A > 0 (unlike molecules repel) bows the total pressure upward and can produce a maximum-pressure azeotrope, while A < 0 bows it downward. Margules activity coefficients: deviations from Raoult's law

Margules wrote the activity coefficients of a binary liquid as power series in mole fraction. The one-parameter form used by MargulesSolution, \ln\gamma_1 = A x_2^2 and \ln\gamma_2 = A x_1^2, turns Raoult's straight lines into curves: A > 0 (unlike molecules repel) bows the total pressure upward and can produce a maximum-pressure azeotrope, while A < 0 bows it downward. The model still obeys the Gibbs-Duhem relation, and each component tends to Henry's law at infinite dilution.

chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.boi: van't Hoff found that a dilute solution's osmotic pressure (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.osmotic_pressure) equals the pressure the solute particles would exert as an ideal gas at the same concentration and temperature. The factor i counts particles per formula unit: 1 for sucrose, about 2 for NaCl. The same factor multiplies the other colligative effects, freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.freezing_point_depression, boiling_point_elevation).
van't Hoff's osmotic pressure law, Pi = iMRT

chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.rao: Raoult's law, P_A = x_A P_A^* (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.mixtures.raoult_vapor_pressure), makes each partial vapor pressure a straight line in liquid mole fraction. Adding the two lines (Dalton's law) gives the total pressure, and BinaryIdealSolution computes the vapor composition, which is always richer in the more volatile component. That enrichment is the basis of fractional distillation.

chemistrykit.thermo.systems.phase_equili: Water's liquid-vapor phase boundary from the integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.phase_equilibria.ClausiusClapeyron), anchored at the normal boiling point. Plotting \ln P against 1/T gives a straight line of slope -\Delta H_{vap}/R; from_two_points recovers \Delta H_{vap} from two measured points, and boiling_point inverts the curve to find the boiling point at altitude.
The Clausius-Clapeyron vapor-pressure curve of water

Gibbs's phase rule, F = C - P + 2 (~chemistrykit.thermo.systems.phase_equilibria.gibbs_phase_rule), says how many intensive variables can change while a set of phases coexists. On a one-component phase diagram, single-phase regions are areas (F=2), two-phase boundaries are curves (F=1), and three phases meet only at a point (F=0). The sketch below draws water's diagram around its triple point (vaporization and sublimation curves from the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, melting line from the Clapeyron slope) and labels each feature with its degrees of freedom.

chemistrykit.thermo.systems.thermochemis: Burning graphite straight to CO_2 releases the same heat as burning it first to CO and then burning the CO. The same principle lets reaction_enthalpy_from_formation compute any reaction enthalpy from tabulated enthalpies of formation, shown here for the combustion of methane.
